translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Yingtian Prefectural Provincial Examination

As the time for the triennial examination approached, Prefect of Yingtian Prefecture, your servant Heng, and Vice Prefect, your servant Zhe, sent a messenger ahead at a gallop to submit a memorial requesting Examiners from the Hanlin Academy. His Majesty commanded your servants Jian and Zhi to go there. The following day, when we took leave of the throne, His Majesty specially favored us with extraordinary honors. Deeply moved upon receiving this grace, your servants grew ever more anxious and fearful, reflecting: Is not the reason His Majesty treats his officials in such an extraordinary manner that He wishes your servants to distinguish the outstanding from the ordinary and seek out extraordinary talent to match His appointments and commissions? We respectfully bore this in mind and dared not forget it. Thereupon, without any further delay, we set out that very day; repeatedly braving dangers without time for self-regard, we arrived after twenty days. title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
臣克謙臣璧臣輔臣謙臣誣臣蘊
各已應聘畢集府中監試官
臣楷臣進則以都臺遴選而
来百凡執事之臣亦必懋簡
以充而提調則臣亨臣哲焉
既入院乃為陳說
聖意聞者咸欣懽鼓舞而相告曰
===
聖天子所以異其禮者示崇重科
目之意也臣等可不知所欽
承顧以尋常眂之乎罔不潔
心澡德圖以共事既而同事
者乃以詰之臣等曰明目張
膽竭精盡瘁以從事於茲固

title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
法若佚之以繩是君子之知
也其言也諂其行也悖其舉
事多悔是小人之知也齊給
便敏而無類雜能旁魄而毋
用折速粹熟而不急不恤是
非不論曲直以期勝人爲意
是役夫之知也聖人君子此
===
其所以自異於常人也小人
役夫此其所以自同於庸衆
也於是乎辭異而不過推類
而不悖聽則合文辨則盡故
正道而辨姦猶櫽隨而命之
同則同之異則異之猶引繩
以持曲直是故邪說不能亂

而不悖聽則合文辨則盡故
正道而辯姦猶以繩而命之

punctuated: 法，若佚之以繩，是君子之知也；其言也諂，其行也悖，其舉事多悔，是小人之知也；齊給便敏而無類，雜能旁魄而毋用，折速粹熟而不急，不恤是非，不論曲直，以期勝人爲意，是役夫之知也。聖人、君子，此其所以自異於常人也；小人、役夫，此其所以自同於庸衆也。於是乎辭異而不過，推類而不悖，聽則合文，辨則盡故。正道而辨姦，猶櫽隨而命之；同則同之，異則異之，猶引繩以持曲直。是故邪說不能亂，
translation_en: … conforms to the model, as if regulated by a plumb line—this is the wisdom of the gentleman. When one's words are flattering, one's actions are perverse, and one's undertakings end mostly in regret—this is the wisdom of the petty man. To be quick-witted, glib, and nimble yet lacking coherent category; to possess miscellaneous skills of wide-ranging scope that are of no practical use; to be trenchant, rapid, and thoroughly practiced in matters of no urgency; and to disregard right and wrong or ignore crooked and straight, intent only on besting others—this is the wisdom of the menial laborer. For the sage and the gentleman, this is whereby they distinguish themselves from ordinary men; for the petty man and the menial laborer, this is whereby they assimilate themselves to the mediocre crowd. Thus, when expressions differ yet do not overstep, when analogies are extended yet do not run counter to reason, when listening accords with pattern and discrimination exhausts the underlying causes, one rectifies the Way and discerns姦 [wickedness/deceit] just as one applies a straightening frame [?] and names things accordingly; one treats the same as the same and the different as different, just as one stretches a plumb line to determine what is crooked and what is straight. Therefore, heterodox doctrines cannot bring confusion, …

text:

已有之曷逃焉眾皆首頷而
退乃合璧雍及畿甸之士與
夫都邑遊居之良而羣試之
其文凡二千卷有奇會其同
而辯其異得百三十有五人
才雖贏不敢妄有所增入遵
===
===

獻諸
天府以聽采於禮闈以視則乎

punctuated: 百家無所竄。茗然無異才則已，有之曷逃焉！」眾皆首頷而退。乃合璧雍及畿甸之士，與夫都邑遊居之良而羣試之，其文凡二千卷有奇，會其同而辯其異，得百三十有五人。才雖贏，不敢妄有所增入，遵定制也。乃會粹其氏名，并簡其尤異者之言而為之錄，將以獻諸天府，以聽采於禮闈，以視則乎來學。錄必有序，鑑敢以齒爵而先焉。竊惟諸士子嚮也居于鄉，混然塗之人也，無以異
translation_en:
… and the hundred schools of thought will have nowhere to hide. Suppose[?] there is no extraordinary talent, then so be it; if there is, how could it escape us!" Everyone nodded in agreement and withdrew.

Thereupon we gathered the scholars of the Directorate of Education and the Metropolitan Area, together with the worthy men residing or traveling in the capital and its counties, and examined them all together. Their papers numbered over two thousand scrolls in total. By bringing together what they had in common and distinguishing what set them apart, we obtained one hundred and thirty-five men. Even though there was a surplus of talent, we did not dare arbitrarily add any more, in compliance with the established quota. We then compiled their names and selected the essays of the most extraordinary among them to make this record, which will be presented to the imperial archives, submitted for selection at the Metropolitan Examination, and shown as a model to future scholars.

Since the record must have a preface, I, Jian, have presumed on the basis of my age and rank to write the opening words. I humbly reflect that in the past, when these scholars lived in their home communities, they mingled indistinguishably with the people in the streets, with nothing to set them apart…

官今又以樸學異能拔之科
目是固有以異也要將捷春
官敭
廷對襃然脫穎而出是豈特異
于鄉之人哉抑固異於天下

translation_en:
… Later, because of their fine talents and extraordinary endowments, they were selected and placed in the government schools; and now again, because of their solid learning and extraordinary abilities, they have been elevated through the examination system—thus they certainly have that by which they are distinguished. Before long, they will triumph under the Ministry of Rites and rise to prominence in the Palace Examination, standing out at the head of the ranks like an awl's point emerging from a bag. How then could they merely be distinguished from the people of their local communities? Indeed, they will certainly be distinguished from the people of the entire empire!

Even so, as for being distinguished: the imperial court treats them as distinguished because of their distinction. If the scholars do not set their minds upon this so as to fully realize its substance, then they are not even equal to petty men and menial laborers. If instead they wish to borrow the name without returning to the reality, this is like lying face down to lick Heaven, or trying to save a hanging man by pulling on his feet; I know that the more they strive, the further off they will be. Alas! "Fine jade and precious pearls, yet they know not how to wear them at their waist; coarse cloth mixed with brocade, yet they know not how to tell them apart"—how lamentable! Surely they must …

title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
忠信以為質端愨以為統禮
義以為文倫類以為理喘而
言臑而動而一可以為法則
斯亦可以言異矣雖然堯舜
與人同耳何以異哉奈何今
之人不皆同也有同焉者斯
異矣咎焉夔焉稷焉契焉斯
===
其同於堯舜者有若人焉得
不謂之異乎諸士子尚思同
乎古而異於今也則甚善矣
毋徒諉曰古之人何可及哉
非所望也非所望也
成化四年歲次戊子秋八月
丁未
alt_text:
忠信以爲質端慤以爲禮
義以爲文倫類以爲理端而
言臑而動而一可以爲法則
斯亦可以言異矣雖然堯舜
與人同耳何以異哉奈何今
之人不皆同也有同焉者斯
異矣各焉夔焉稷焉契焉斯
===
其間於堯舜者有若人焉得
不謂之異乎諸士子尚思同
乎古而異於今也則甚善矣
毋徒諉曰古之人何可及哉
非所望也非所望也
成化四年歲次戊子秋八月
丁未
punctuated:
忠信以為質，端愨以為統，禮義以為文，倫類以為理，喘而言，臑而動，而一可以為法則，斯亦可以言異矣。雖然，堯、舜與人同耳，何以異哉？奈何今之人不皆同也，有同焉者，斯異矣。咎焉、夔焉、稷焉、契焉，斯其同於堯、舜者，有若人，焉得不謂之異乎？諸士子尚思同乎古而異於今也，則甚善矣！毋徒諉曰：「古之人何可及哉！」非所望也，非所望也。
成化四年歲次戊子秋八月丁未，
translation_en:
…take loyalty and trustworthiness as their substance, uprightness and sincerity as their guiding thread, ritual and righteousness as their refinement, and human relationships and moral categories as their ordering principle—so that every breath and word, every movement and action, may without exception serve as a model and standard—then this too may be called extraordinary. Even so, Yao and Shun were the same as other men; wherein lay their difference? Alas, people of the present day are not all the same as they were; thus, when someone is the same as they were, that person is considered extraordinary! Gao Yao, Kui, Hou Ji, and Xie—these were the ones who were the same as Yao and Shun. If there are men such as these today, how could one not call them extraordinary? Should all you scholars aspire to be the same as the ancients and thereby stand apart from the present age, that would be admirable indeed! Do not merely make excuses, saying, "How can the men of antiquity ever be equaled!" That is not what is hoped of you; that is not what is hoped of you.

Four Books

"To those whose talents are above mediocrity, the highest subjects may be announced. To those who are below mediocrity, the highest subjects may not be announced."

"Study it extensively, inquire into it accurately, think over it carefully, sift it clearly, and practice it earnestly. While there is anything not studied, or while in what has been studied there is anything not yet mastered, do not intermit. While there is anything not inquired into, or while in what has been inquired into there is anything not yet known, do not intermit. While there is anything not thought over, or while in what has been thought over there is anything not yet apprehended, do not intermit. While there is anything not sifted, or while in what has been sifted there is anything not yet made clear, do not intermit. While there is anything not practiced, or while in what has been practiced there is anything not yet done earnestly, do not intermit."

"There is no part of himself which a man does not love, and as he loves all, so he must nourish all. There is not an inch of skin which he does not love, and so there is not an inch of skin which he will not nourish. For examining whether his way of nourishing be good or not, what other rule is there? It is simply to be found in his own choice. Some parts of the body are noble, and some ignoble; some great, and some small. The great must not be injured for the small, nor the noble for the ignoble. He who nourishes the little belonging to him is a little man, and he who nourishes the great is a great man."

I have never failed to sigh with admiration that the meeting of an enlightened ruler and worthy ministers is a rare encounter that happens once in a thousand years. Thereafter, I humbly read the opening chapter of the Grand Pronouncements (Da Gao) of our Grand Progenitor, Emperor Gao [the Hongwu Emperor], which says: "In antiquity, ministers who were able to associate with their ruler exhausted their loyalty to bring their ruler to perfection; in eating, drinking, dreaming, and sleeping, they never forgot governance. title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
誥詞者誰歟其人其行可以追配於賡
歌之人否歟諸士子遊歌泮庠是
訓是行必能熟複而詳識之矣請
陳於篇毋泛毋隱
問天下治忽係宰相君德成就責經
筵此二者天下之重任歷代所體
貌者也然世殊事異不可槩論夫
輔君以致治者宰相之職也若伊
===
周之輔相尚矣漢稱蕭曹為冠以
開創之功也然誅呂安劉擁昭立
宣者不與焉豈刀筆黃老之流反
賢乎唐稱房杜為首以貞觀之治
也然再造唐室係國安危者不與
焉豈傳無可載之功者顧優乎宋
之韓范富歐世固以並稱然亦有
優劣可議歟其有與富韓齊名者

誥詞者誰歟？其人其行，可以追配於賡歌之人否歟？諸士子遊歌泮庠，是訓是行，必能熟複而詳識之矣。請陳於篇，毋泛毋隱。
問：天下治忽係宰相，君德成就責經筵，此二者，天下之重任，歷代所體貌者也。然世殊事異，不可槩論。夫輔君以致治者，宰相之職也。若伊、周之輔相尚矣。漢稱蕭、曹為冠，以開創之功也；然誅呂安劉、擁昭立宣者不與焉，豈刀筆、黃老之流反賢乎？唐稱房、杜為首，以貞觀之治也；然再造唐室、係國安危者不與焉，豈傳無可載之功者顧優乎？宋之韓、范、富、歐，世固以並稱，然亦有優劣可議歟？其有與富、韓齊名者，
translation_en:
…the words of the imperial admonitions, who were they? Can those men and their deeds be matched with the men of the responsive songs of antiquity? You scholars, studying and singing in the state schools, taking these as your teachings and putting them into practice, have surely reviewed them thoroughly and understood them in detail. Please set forth your views in your essays, neither speaking in vague generalities nor holding anything back.

Question: The order or disorder of the realm depends upon the Grand Councilor (zaixiang), and the perfection of the ruler's virtue is the responsibility of the Classics Mat (jingyan). These two are the heaviest responsibilities in the world, and those whom successive dynasties have treated with high courtesy and respect. Yet ages differ and affairs vary, so they cannot be discussed with a single generalization. Now, to assist the ruler in bringing about good governance is the duty of the Grand Councilor. The ministerial assistance of Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou is of course supreme. In the Han dynasty, Xiao He and Cao Can were acclaimed as the foremost because of their merit in founding the dynasty; yet those who exterminated the Lü clan and secured the Liu house [such as Chen Ping and Zhou Bo], or who supported Emperor Zhao and enthroned Emperor Xuan [such as Huo Guang], were not included in that rank—could it be that men from the ranks of petty legal clerks and followers of Huang-Lao were actually worthier? In the Tang dynasty, Fang Xuanling and Du 如晦 (Du Ruhui) were acclaimed as the first because of the good governance of the Zhenguan reign; yet those who restored the Tang house and upon whom the safety and peril of the state depended [such as Di Renjie, Yao Chong, Song Jing, or Guo Ziyi] were not included—could it be that those whose biographies lacked specific achievements to record were instead superior? In the Song dynasty, Han Qi, Fan Zhongyan, Fu Bi, and Ouyang Xiu have indeed been named together by the world, yet are there also relative merits and shortcomings among them that can be debated? As for the one who shared equal fame with Fu Bi and Han Qi…

text:
果誰歟既云齊名而世不並稱之
何歟講學以輔德經筵之職也若
說旦之啓沃卓矣漢自石渠白虎
稱制臨決經筵始有定所也然君
德果有成乎其視講論經理夜分
不寐與夫樸學不好博士不講者

translation_en:
… who indeed was it? Since they were said to be equal in fame, why did the world not name them together?

Lecturing on learning to assist in cultivating virtue is the duty of the Classics Colloquium (Jingyan). The enlightening counsel of Fu Yue 傅說 and the Duke of Zhou (Zhougong Dan 周公旦) was trulyeminent. In the Han dynasty, from the time the emperors personally attended the Stone Canal Pavilion (Shiquge 石渠閣) and White Tiger Hall (Baihuguan 白虎觀) to pronounce final decisions by imperial decree, the Classics Colloquium first had a fixed location; yet was the ruler's virtue truly brought to completion? How does that compare in worthiness to discussing the principles of the Classics past midnight without sleeping, or to having no fondness for plain learning while the Erudites (Boshi) ceased lecturing? In the Tang dynasty, from the time Ma Zhou 馬周 and Chu Suiliang 褚遂良 entered the inner court and officials were appointed to the Academy of Scholarly Worthies (Jixianyuan 集賢院), the Classics Colloquium first had regular offices; yet did the ruler's virtue truly benefit from it? How does that compare in superiority to discussing antiquity and the present late into the night while forgetting fatigue, or to paying heed to the ancient canons and amusing oneself with books and histories? In the Song dynasty, the Classics Colloquium had no fixed location and the Lecturers (Jiangguan) had no fixed quota; yet can the details of this be recounted? When someone specially recited three sentences and the ruler sighed in admiration, and then recited six more sentences and the ruler nodded in approval, from what book were those passages actually taken? And once the ruler had gained something from them, was it ever extended into actual practice?

translation_en:
…the Sovereign alone. Yet can those who occupy the positions of chief counselors also be held responsible for security and peril? The Emperor's sacred virtue is Heaven-endowed, so that it indeed seems he has no need for study; yet can those who bear the responsibility of exhortation and lecturing truly be of aid in even one part in ten thousand? All you gentlemen aspire to make your ruler and people like those in the times of Yao and Shun; when in the future you are employed in positions of authority and perform your duties, whom among the ancients will you take as your model? Please set this forth in full, so that we may observe the learning you have accumulated.

Question: Military affairs are the great business of the state, and generals and commanders are the vital pivot of the military. The security or peril of the empire and the state hinges upon a single mobilization, and the lives of the Six Armies and the myriad multitude hang upon a single man. Therefore troops must not be lightly mobilized, and still less may command of them be entrusted to the wrong man. Yet troops must be trained before they become elite, and generals must be selected before the right ones are obtained. As for the methods of training troops and the ways of selecting generals, which of them grasp the essentials? Let us take those of antiquity who excelled as generals and discuss their merits and shortcomings with you gentlemen. Now, he who composed a book in thirteen chapters—subtle, mysterious, profound, and secret, with inexhaustible transformations—was admirable indeed; why then was it also said of him that he did not follow the proper Way? title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
通萬物拓地千里似矣何又謂其
難行於世歟扁舟五湖辟穀棄事
其功成身退一也何又有優劣之
論歟不學兵法然六出匈奴所向
輒克其故何歟能讀父書然一為
趙將輒破趙軍其失何歟兵法果
不可學歟戰國西漢勇將多矣所
稱者胡止二人歟豈其能勇於義

translation_en: …comprehended the myriad things, and expanded territory by a thousand li—this seems plausible enough; yet why is it also said to be difficult to put into practice in the world? Floating away in a skiff on the Five Lakes, and abstaining from grain while abandoning worldly affairs: in retiring after achieving success, they were one and the same; why then are there discussions ranking one above the other? Not studying the art of war, yet marching out six times against the Xiongnu and conquering wherever he went—what was the reason for this? Being able to read his father's books, yet the moment he became a general of Zhao, having the army of Zhao routed—where did his failure lie? Can the art of war truly not be learned? In the Warring States and Western Han there were many brave generals; why are only two men singled out for praise? Could it be that they were capable of bravery in the cause of righteousness? Are they truly worthy of emulation or not? Dwelling long in wealth and honor, preserving merit and fame from beginning to end, it seemed as though he accomplished nothing; why then was he said to possess the Way of a gentleman? What Way was his Way, in truth? Holding the long reins to control from afar and dragging things out over months and years, he sat idly by and lost tactical opportunities; why then was he said to have grasped the art of defending against the western barbarians? What art was his art, in truth? Never recklessly killing a single man, versus treacherously burying alive a hundred thousand surrendered soldiers—how different were their intentions? And was Heaven's retribution and reward for them also different? Allying with Wu to resist Wei, and holding Shu while proclaiming the Han: in praising him as a talent fit to assist a true king, antiquity and the present speak with a single…

title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
詞其人可謂偉矣何以不能成功
再造王室勲業巍然以身為天下
安危其人可謂烈矣何以不可為
法是皆為將之良光昭簡冊者夫
有文事者必有武備他日倘有閫
外之寄如宋韓范諸公則於前數
君子誰可為法誰可為戒尚當跡
其人究其實而詳論之以觀二三
===
子用世之志
問民惟邦本本固邦寧然歲有豐凶
物有盈縮而民之安否係焉民之
安危邦之寧否關焉善為政者不
可不致慮於此也今之為歲春夏
則恒暘秋冬則恒雨豈政教失道
有以致之歟抑陰陽自有定數歟
昔堯之水湯之旱或九年七年二

其人究其實而詳論之以觀二三

物有盈縮而民之安否係焉民之
安危邦之寧否關焉善爲政者不
可不致慮於此也今之爲歲春夏

詞，其人可謂偉矣，何以不能成功？再造王室，勲業巍然，以身為天下安危，其人可謂烈矣，何以不可為法？是皆為將之良，光昭簡冊者。夫有文事者必有武備，他日倘有閫外之寄，如宋韓、范諸公，則於前數君子，誰可為法？誰可為戒？尚當跡其人，究其實，而詳論之，以觀二三子用世之志。
問：民惟邦本，本固邦寧。然歲有豐凶，物有盈縮，而民之安否係焉；民之安危，邦之寧否關焉。善為政者，不可不致慮於此也。今之為歲，春夏則恒暘，秋冬則恒雨，豈政教失道有以致之歟？抑陰陽自有定數歟？昔堯之水、湯之旱，或九年、七年，二
translation_en:
…unanimous acclaim—such a man may indeed be called great; why then was he unable to achieve success? Rebuilding the royal house, with towering merit and achievements, and bearing the safety and peril of the empire upon his own person—such a man may indeed be called heroic; why then can he not be taken as a model? These were all fine generals whose glory shines in the historical records. Now, those who have civil affairs must also have military preparations. If one day you are entrusted with a command beyond the frontier gates, like Master Han [Han Qi 韓琦] and Master Fan [Fan Zhongyan 范仲淹] of the Song dynasty, then among the several gentlemen mentioned above, whom may you take as a model, and whom as a warning? You should trace their lives, investigate their realities, and discuss them in detail, so that we may observe your aspirations, gentlemen, to be of service to the world.

Question: The people are the foundation of the state; when the foundation is firm, the state is at peace. Yet harvests have years of abundance and dearth, and resources have times of surplus and scarcity, upon which the security of the people depends; and upon the security or peril of the people, the peace or instability of the state hinges. Those who excel at governance cannot fail to devote their thoughts to this. In the present year, there was constant sunshine in spring and summer, and constant rain in autumn and winter. Could it be that some failure in the way of governance and moral instruction has brought this about? Or do yin and yang naturally have their fixed cycles? In antiquity, the floods of Yao 堯 and the droughts of Tang 湯 lasted nine years or seven years; those two…

title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
聖人豈失道者歟然其民不聞有
菜色果何道以致之歟周禮荒政
十有二可謂善矣或者乃小之何
歟大者果何在歟茲欲均歲功於
豐凶救人命於凍餒抑別有其術
歟世之為政者不此之慮方且爬
梳宿逋久負以為聚斂之能嚴刑
酷法以為征輸之善其果何心歟
===
方今
皇上視民如傷從諫弗咈何故都無一人
以此言於
上歟豈以為細故而不足言歟茲欲沮其
聚斂之謀省其征輸之酷使瀕危
之民轉之於衽席之上飢餒之眾
置之於饜飫之中必有善處之道
明以告我將以聞於

translation_en:
… Sages ones who had lost the Way? Yet it was never heard that their people had the sallow complexions of hunger—by what way indeed was this achieved? The twelve famine-relief policies in the Rites of Zhou (Zhouli) may be called good, yet some consider them minor—why is that? Wherein, indeed, does the greater way lie? If we now wish to equalize the yearly harvests between abundance and dearth, and save people's lives from freezing and starvation, is there perhaps some other method? Those who govern in the world today do not give thought to this; instead, they comb through old arrears and long-standing debts, taking this as competence in revenue collection, and use severe punishments and harsh laws, taking this as excellence in tax extraction—what could possibly be on their minds?

At present, the August Emperor looks upon the people as if they were wounded and follows remonstrances without opposition. For what reason is there not a single person who speaks of this to the Emperor? Could it be that they consider it a trifling matter not worth mentioning? Now, if we wish to thwart those schemes of revenue extraction and reduce the harshness of tax collection, so as to turn the people who are on the brink of peril onto the safety of their sleeping mats, and place the starving multitudes into a state of full satiation, there must be a good way to manage it. Explain it clearly to me, so that I may report it to…

title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
上而行之毋徒辭出位之嫌而有所悋也
問孔子曰善人為邦百年亦可以勝
殘去殺矣又曰王者必世而後仁
甚矣教化之洽非一日積也洪惟
我
朝
列聖相承施政設教百有餘年王者之化
宜乎浹於世矣豈特善人之效而
已哉然當時之務尚有可議試與
諸君商其一二今之任賢去邪非
無法也然每有刺舉賢否同科將
欲銓選精而黜陟當其道何由今
之足國裕民非無制也然一有調
發公私皆困將欲國用充而民食
足其計何出軍功不一也陞賞有
差然冒濫者衆何以使賞必當功

===
已哉然當時之務尚有可議試與
諸君商其一二今之任賢去邪非
無法也然每有剌舉賢否同科將
欲銓選精而黜陟當其道何由今
之足國裕民非無制也然一有調
發公私皆困將欲國用充而民食
足其計何出軍功不一也陞賞有
差然冒濫者衆何以使賞必當功
punctuated:
上而行之，毋徒辭出位之嫌而有所悋也。
問：孔子曰：「善人為邦百年，亦可以勝殘去殺矣。」又曰：「王者必世而後仁。」甚矣，教化之洽，非一日積也！洪惟我朝列聖相承，施政設教，百有餘年，王者之化，宜乎浹於世矣，豈特善人之效而已哉！然當時之務，尚有可議，試與諸君商其一二。今之任賢去邪，非無法也，然每有刺舉，賢否同科，將欲銓選精而黜陟當，其道何由？今之足國裕民，非無制也，然一有調發，公私皆困，將欲國用充而民食足，其計何出？軍功不一也，陞賞有差，然冒濫者衆，何以使賞必當功
translation_en:
… the Emperor and put it into practice. Do not merely decline out of fear of overstepping your position and hold back in your replies.

Question: Confucius said, "If good men were to govern a state in succession for a hundred years, they would be able to overcome cruelty and dispense with capital punishment." He also said, "Even with a true king, it would certainly take a generation before humaneness is achieved." Indeed, the pervasive spread of moral transformation is not accumulated in a single day! When we reflect deeply upon how the successive sacred emperors of our Dynasty have inherited the throne one after another, administering governance and establishing moral instruction for more than a hundred years, the transformative influence of a true king ought to have thoroughly permeated the world—how could it merely be the efficacy of "good men" and nothing more! Yet among the affairs of the present day, there are still matters open to discussion; let us try to deliberate on one or two of them with you gentlemen.

In the present day, employing the worthy and removing the wicked is not without laws; yet whenever there are impeachments and recommendations, the worthy and the unworthy are placed in the same category. If we wish to make personnel selection precise and demotions and promotions appropriate, by what way may this be achieved? In the present day, enriching the state and providing abundantly for the people is not without regulations; yet as soon as there is arequisition or mobilization, both public finances and private households are exhausted. If we wish for state expenditures to be well-supplied and the people's food to be sufficient, from where shall such a plan come? Military merits are not uniform, and promotions and rewards are graded accordingly; yet those who falsely claim or excessively receive them are numerous. How can we ensure that rewards always match actual merit…

title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
歟刑罰未允也審錄有
詔然幸免者多何以使罰必當罪歟學
校人材所出也然所習或遺本而
逐末若何而使本末俱習賢才不
乏歟言路耳目所寄也然所陳多
舍大而摭小若何而使大小畢陳
言路無壅歟舉行鄉飲所以教民
睦也然告訐之風紛如今欲使民
===
知遜弟爭訟不興果有方歟申明
禮制所以定民志也然奢僭之俗
靡然今欲使民循禁章服色不亂
亦有道歟之數者皆當今之已行
而未效者也將襲而行之歟則法
日以弊將變而通之歟則法固具
在古人有言識時務者在俊傑諸
士子皆負俊傑之名應興賢之詔

===
知孫𢧐爭訟不興罣有方歟申明
禮制所以定民志也然奢僭之俗
靡然今欲使民循禁章服色不亂
亦有道歟之數者皆當今之已行
而未效者也將襲而行之歟則法
日以弊將變而通之歟則法固具
在古人有言識時務者在俊傑諸
士子皆負俊傑之名應興賢之詔
punctuated: 歟？刑罰未允也，審錄有詔，然幸免者多，何以使罰必當罪歟？學校，人材所出也，然所習或遺本而逐末，若何而使本末俱習、賢才不乏歟？言路，耳目所寄也，然所陳多舍大而摭小，若何而使大小畢陳、言路無壅歟？舉行鄉飲，所以教民睦也，然告訐之風紛如，今欲使民知遜弟、爭訟不興，果有方歟？申明禮制，所以定民志也，然奢僭之俗靡然，今欲使民循禁章、服色不亂，亦有道歟？之數者，皆當今之已行而未效者也。將襲而行之歟，則法日以弊；將變而通之歟，則法固具在。古人有言：「識時務者在俊傑。」諸士子皆負俊傑之名，應興賢之詔，
translation_en: …? Punishments and penalties are not yet equitable: there are imperial decrees for the review of judicial records, yet those who escape punishment by luck are many; how can one ensure that penalties always fit the crimes? Schools are where men of talent emerge, yet what they study sometimes neglects the fundamentals to pursue the superficial; how can one ensure that both fundamentals and secondary matters are practiced and that worthy talents are not lacking? The avenue of remonstrance is where the ruler's ears and eyes are entrusted, yet what is presented mostly sets aside great matters to pick up trivial ones; how can one ensure that both great and small matters are fully set forth and the avenue of remonstrance is unobstructed? Holding the district symposium is the means to teach the people harmony, yet the custom of making accusations and exposing others' secrets is rampant; if today we wish to make the people know deference and fraternal respect so that litigation does not arise, is there indeed a method? Clarifying the ritual regulations is the means to settle the people's ambitions, yet customs of extravagance and usurpation prevail everywhere; if today we wish to make the people abide by the prohibitions and statutes so that styles and colors of dress are not thrown into confusion, is there also a way? These several matters are all things that have already been put into practice at present without yet achieving results. Shall we follow along and carry them out as before? Then the laws will grow more defective by the day. Shall we alter and adapt them? Then the laws are in fact already complete and in place. The ancients had a saying: "Those who understand the affairs of the times are the outstanding heroes." All you scholars bear the reputation of outstanding heroes and have responded to the imperial decree promoting the worthy; …

"To those who are above average, one may speak of higher things; to those who are below average, one may not speak of higher things." [Analects 6.21]

He En 賀恩

Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Hou 侯: This topic concerns the Sage's discussion of the method of teaching people, and "above" and "below" refer to both natural endowment and scholarly effort. Comment by Examiner Academician Chen 陳: Plain, solid, and grasps the main point.

Because people's talent and learning cannot be without higher and lower levels, when one teaches others, one must follow their higher and lower levels. For the endowment of talent and nature, and the achievement of study and inquiry, differ from person to person. If a teacher does not follow their higher and lower levels and instead speaks to them all in the same way, how can he improve people? In the past, when our Master discussed the method of teaching people, his meaning was as if to say: The Way has no division between subtle and coarse, yet people have higher and lower levels; how then could teaching alone be without gradations? title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
焉有聽受之地故可以語性命道德之懿使之優入
於聖域學焉有造詣之功故可以語精義入神之妙
使之日進於高明夫所以語之以上者非私厚之也
因其可語而語之耳又有人焉資稟不及於中人而
或優於戇愚學問未至於中人而或流乎庸懦所謂
中人以下者也斯人也質焉無領悟之由固未可強
而語之以微妙之說使之茫然無所喻學焉無進脩
之力尤不可驟而告之以精深之理使之憺然無所
得夫所以不語之以上者非吝教之也因其不可語
===
而弗之語耳吁可以語而不語則彼無由以入道不
可語而語之則彼將妄意而躐等雖然聖人無棄人
豈終不語之哉亦因其所至漸而語之耳君子之教
焉可誣也抑嘗因是言而徵諸聖門之教矣克己復
禮惟顏淵得聞之主敬行恕惟仲弓得聞之至於司
馬牛樊遲之問仁或告以其言也訒或告以先難後
獲而克復敬恕之說弗及焉是知回也雍也中人以
上者也牛與遲其中人以下者乎聖人教人各因其
材於斯可見不然一貫之旨性與天道之言何子貢

… has the capacity to listen and receive; therefore one may speak to him of the excellence of human nature, destiny, the Way, and virtue, enabling him to enter with ease into the realm of the sages. In his learning, he has the achievement of deep attainment; therefore one may speak to him of the subtlety of investigating meanings to the point of entering the numinous, enabling him to advance daily toward lofty illumination. Now, the reason one speaks to him of higher things is not out of partiality or favor toward him; it is simply that because he can be spoken to of them, one speaks to him of them.

Then there is another person: though his natural endowment falls short of the middling person, he is perhaps superior to the simple and foolish; though his learning has not yet reached that of the middling person, he perhaps drifts into mediocrity and timidity. This is what is meant by those who are below the middling level. With such a person, in his natural substance he lacks the means for comprehension, so one certainly cannot force upon him subtle and abstruse doctrines, leaving him bewildered and without understanding; in his learning he lacks the strength for advancing and cultivating himself, so one especially cannot abruptly tell him of profound and recondite principles, leaving him blank [?] and having gained nothing. Now, the reason one does not speak to him of higher things is not because one is stingy in teaching him; it is simply that because he cannot be spoken to of them, one does not speak of them to him.

Alas! If someone can be spoken to of higher things and one does not speak of them, then he will have no way to enter the Way; if someone cannot be spoken to of them and one speaks of them to him, then he will form wild conjectures and skip over the proper steps. Even so, the sage abandons no one—how could he never speak to them of such things to the very end? He simply follows what they have attained and speaks to them gradually. How could the teaching of the noble man be falsified?

Moreover, on the basis of these words I have tested this against the teachings of the Sage's school. "Overcoming the self and returning to ritual propriety"—only Yan Yuan 顏淵 was able to hear of it; "holding fast to reverence and practicing reciprocity"—only Zhonggong 仲弓 was able to hear of it. As for Sima Niu 司馬牛 and Fan Chi 樊遲 asking about humaneness, one was told that "his speech is hesitant," and the other was told to "put difficulties first and success afterward," while the doctrines of overcoming the self and returning to propriety, or of reverence and reciprocity, were not mentioned to them. From this we know that Hui 回 [Yan Yuan] and Yong 雍 [Zhonggong] were those above the middling level, while Niu and Chi were perhaps those below the middling level! title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
氣禀或異故凡誠有未至者其可不學知而利行乎
是故學不博則無以備事物之理故必博而學之焉
學博矣然後能參互之以得所疑而有問問不審則
無以盡師友之情故必審而問之焉問審矣然後能
反覆之以啓其端而可思而思之必謹焉思之謹則
精而不雜故能有所自得而可施於辯而辯之必明
焉辯之明則斷而不差故能無所疑惑而可見於行
也既學問矣而不施之踐履則是徒取於人無益也
既思辯矣而不措諸躬行則是徒求於心無得也故
===
必躬行實踐不使一毫人欲之私得以奪乎天理之
正此學知利行知仁之事也誠之之功可謂至矣然
如是而猶有未能可不加困知勉行之勇乎是故不
學不問則已然既學之問之而有弗能弗知則豈可
舍之而弗理必學而至於能問而至於知而後已焉
不思不辯則已然既思之辯之而有弗得弗明則豈
可措之而弗治必思而至於得辯而至於明而後止
也不以學問見於行則已行之則必極其篤不可半
途而廢也不以思辯見諸行則已行之則必要其成

punctuated: 氣禀或異，故凡誠有未至者，其可不學知而利行乎？是故學不博，則無以備事物之理，故必博而學之焉。學博矣，然後能參互之以得所疑而有問。問不審，則無以盡師友之情，故必審而問之焉。問審矣，然後能反覆之以啓其端而可思，而思之必謹焉。思之謹，則精而不雜，故能有所自得而可施於辯，而辯之必明焉。辯之明，則斷而不差，故能無所疑惑而可見於行也。既學問矣，而不施之踐履，則是徒取於人，無益也；既思辯矣，而不措諸躬行，則是徒求於心，無得也。故必躬行實踐，不使一毫人欲之私，得以奪乎天理之正。此學知利行、知仁之事也，誠之之功可謂至矣。然如是而猶有未能，可不加困知勉行之勇乎？是故不學不問則已，然既學之、問之，而有弗能、弗知，則豈可舍之而弗理？必學而至於能、問而至於知而後已焉。不思不辯則已，然既思之、辯之，而有弗得、弗明，則豈可措之而弗治？必思而至於得、辯而至於明而後止也。不以學問見於行則已，行之則必極其篤，不可半途而廢也；不以思辯見諸行則已，行之則必要其成，
translation_en: …their qi endowment may differ; therefore, for anyone whose sincerity has not yet reached perfection, how could they not learn in order to know, and practice because it is beneficial? For this reason, if one's learning is not extensive, there is no way to encompass the principles of affairs and things; therefore, one must study extensively. Once learning is extensive, only then can one cross-reference things to discover what is doubtful and have questions to ask. If questioning is notSearching and thorough, there is no way to exhaust the insights of teachers and friends; therefore, one must inquire thoroughly. Once questioning is thorough, only then can one turn things over repeatedly to open up their beginnings and be able to reflect, and in reflecting one must be careful. When reflection is careful, it is refined and unmixed; thus one can attain personal realization and apply it to discrimination, and in discriminating one must be clear. When discrimination is clear, judgment is decisive and without error; thus one can be free of all doubt and manifest it in action. Having studied and inquired, if one does not apply it in actual practice, it is merely taking from others in vain, which is of no benefit; having reflected and discriminated, if one does not put it into personal action, it is merely seeking within one's own mind in vain, which yields no attainment. Therefore, one must personally act and earnestly practice, not allowing a single hair's breadth of selfish human desire to usurp the correctness of Heavenly Principle. This is the business of knowing through learning and practicing because it is beneficial—that is, of wisdom and humanity; the effort of attaining sincerity can thus be called complete. Yet if, even so, there remains something one is not yet able to do, how could one not add the courage of knowing through painful effort and practicing with strenuous exertion? Therefore, if one does not study or inquire, let it be; yet once one has studied and inquired, if there is anything one is not yet capable of or does not yet understand, how could one abandon it and leave it unattended? One must study until capable, and inquire until understanding, and only then stop. If one does not reflect or discriminate, let it be; yet once one has reflected and discriminated, if there is anything one has not yet grasped or made clear, how could one set it aside and leave it unexamined? One must reflect until grasping it, and discriminate until making it clear, and only then cease. If one does not manifest study and inquiry in action, let it be; if one acts upon them, one must carry it to the utmost earnestness and must not abandon it halfway. If one does not manifest reflection and discrimination in action, let it be; if one acts upon them, one must carry it through to completion, …

translation_en:
… and one must not stop halfway along the path. This is the business of learning through hard toil and practicing with strenuous effort—that is, of courage. What could possibly be added to such effort in attaining sincerity? How could those of later generations who wish to make their own persons sincere not seek it right here? Moreover, if we examine this chapter, where the Sage answers Duke Ai’s (Ai Gong 哀公) question about governance: the preceding text has already stated, “Sincerity is the Way of Heaven; attaining sincerity is the Way of Man.” One who is naturally sincere is indeed a sage born with knowledge who practices it with ease, whereas one who attains sincerity engages in the work of a worthy; this is the reality of that attainment. If a person is truly capable of this, then even the foolish can become enlightened and the weak can become strong. Had Duke Ai been able to follow the Sage’s words and put them into practice, the Way of King Wen, King武 (Wu), and the Duke of Zhou (Zhou Gong 周公) would have been nothing more than this. Alas, what a pity that he did not awaken to it! Could Zisi 子思 have lacked a deeper purpose in citing these words to follow upon the account of King Wen, King Wu, and the Duke of Zhou?

“A man loves all parts of his person without exception. Loving all parts without exception, he nourishes all parts without exception. There is not a single foot or inch of his skin that he does not love, and so there is not a single foot or inch of his skin that he does not nourish. As for the means of examining whether his way of nourishing is good or not good, is it anything other than this? He simply takes the standard from within himself. Among the parts of the body, some are noble and some base, some great and some small. One must not harm the great for the sake of the small, nor harm the noble for the sake of the base. He who nourishes the small parts becomes a petty man; he who nourishes the great parts becomes a great man.” [Mencius 6A.14]
By Wu Yin 吳寅.
Comment by Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor (xundao) Ye 葉: For days on end in this examination ward, I have been reading papers, and most of those writing on this topic used tedious, fragmented phrasing that made one weary to look at them. Late in the process I came upon this essay: its opening analysis of the theme (po) is concise and clear, and its exposition (jiang) is well-ordered and fluent. Reading it beneath the green lamp, my mind and eyes suddenly felt refreshed and clear. It ought to be copied out and published as a model for later students.

Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Wang: Because the topic is long, the opening statement (po) is difficult to summarize concisely, and the exposition (jiang) in most papers tends to be wordy and redundant. Only this essay captures the theme in a single opening statement without the slightest omission, while its exposition is clear and detailed section by section. Truly it is a fine work from this examination ward. Admirable, admirable!

Comment by Examiner Academician Reader-in-Waiting Yin: In the examination hall, essays on the Mencius topic like this one were exceedingly rare; therefore we have singled it out for publication.

Comment by Examiner Academician Chen: Among the expositions on the Mencius, there were scarcely any fine pieces. This essay alone excels, standing quite apart from those that merely piece together trivialities.

All parts of the body are loved and nourished without omission, yet whether that nourishment is good or not must be examined within oneself; the parts of the body are distinguished into weighty and light—which gives cause for caution—and upon this depends whether a person is worthy or unworthy. Now, one who loves his own person certainly leaves no part of it unnourished. Yet since the parts of the body differ in importance and ways of nourishing them differ in goodness, does not a person's worthiness or unworthiness depend upon what he nourishes?

Of old, Mencius's meaning was that in a person's single body all the hundred parts are complete: when one loves it, one loves them all alike, so that nothing loved is left uncovered; and once one knows what one loves, one necessarily nourishes them all alike, so that nothing nourished is left unprovided for. Even a foot of skin is most slight, yet it is all the harmonious vitality entrusted by Heaven and Earth and certainly ought to be loved—so not even a foot of skin goes unnourished. A square inch of skin is smaller still, yet it is all the bodily frame bequeathed by one's parents and equally ought to be loved—so not even an inch of skin goes unnourished.

Although the love and nourishment are the same, in nourishing there must be discernment; hence in what one nourishes there is that which is good and that which is not good. If one wishes to know whether it is good, what need is there to seek elsewhere? One need only reflect upon oneself to examine what one treats as weighty. If one wishes to know whether it is not good, why wait to look elsewhere? One need only draw upon oneself to examine what one treats as light. Nothing is weightier than the mind and will: the mind and will are able to think and deliberate, and serve as master over the mouth and belly—are they not the noble and great parts of the body…

punctuated:
之貴而大者乎？輕莫輕於口腹，口腹則有嗜欲而為心志之役，非體之賤而小者乎？苟養之者使以心志從口腹，則是小害大矣，固不可也；以飢渴為心害，則是賤害貴矣，尤不可也。惟小不可以害大，故專以飲食養口腹者，則人心以危，道心以微，得不謂之小人乎？惟賤不可以害貴，故專以義理養心志者，則道心為主，人心聽命，得不謂之大人乎？吁！大人小人相去甚遠，而其分乃在所養善否之間。然則欲為大人之歸者，其可不審而徒事口腹邪？抑考之孟子他日答公都子之問，又曰：「從其大體為大人，從其小體為小人。」則又以耳目心志為小大。蓋溺於口腹之欲，固足以害其心志；汨於耳目之私，尤足以蔽其心思。此其言雖殊，而實互相發也。遏人欲而存天理，蓋惓惓焉，此孟子所以有功於前聖也歟！

易義
終日乾乾，行事也；或躍在淵，自試也；飛龍在天，上治也。

translation_en:
… the noble and great part of the body? Nothing is less important than the mouth and belly; the mouth and belly have cravings and desires and serve the mind and will—are they not the base and petty part of the body? If in nourishing them one causes the mind and will to follow the mouth and belly, then the petty harms the great, which is certainly impermissible; if one allows hunger and thirst to become a harm to the mind, then the base harms the noble, which is even more impermissible. Because the petty must not harm the great, those who devote themselves solely to nourishing the mouth and belly with food and drink render the human mind precarious and the moral mind subtle—can they be called anything other than petty men? Because the base must not harm the noble, those who devote themselves solely to nourishing the mind and will with moral principles make the moral mind the master while the human mind obeys its commands—can they be called anything other than great men? Ah! Great men and petty men are worlds apart, yet the distinction between them lies simply in whether what they nourish is good or not. That being so, how can one who wishes to attain the state of a great man fail to examine this carefully and merely busy himself with the mouth and belly? Furthermore, if we examine Mencius's reply on another day to the question of Gongduzi, he also said: "Those who follow the part of themselves that is great are great men; those who follow the part of themselves that is petty are petty men." There, in turn, he treated the ears and eyes and the mind and will as the petty and the great. For to drown in the desires of the mouth and belly is certainly enough to harm one's mind and will, while to be submerged in the selfish attractions of the ears and eyes is even more sufficient to obscure one's thoughts. Although his words in these two passages differ, in reality they illuminate one another. In curbing human desires and preserving Heavenly Principle, how earnest and untiring he was! Is this not why Mencius rendered such meritorious service to the former sages?

Expositions on the Book of Changes (Yi)
"All day long active and vigilant": this refers to the advancement of deeds. "Perhaps leaping in the deep": this refers to testing oneself. "The flying dragon is in the heavens": this refers to governing from above.

聖人三舉乾卦爻辭而釋之以見聖德以漸而顯也
夫聖德以漸而顯者因時位以漸而進也文言聖人
於乾卦爻詞三舉之而各申其義得無意乎且乾之
諸爻皆有聖人之德也而九三之爻周公係以終日
乾乾矣而夫子又申之以行事何耶盖以九三居下
之上重剛不中所當事者進德而已故終日憂勤行
夫進德之事而不息所當行者修業而已故終日惕
厲行夫修業之事而無間此其所以行事也夫行事

The Sage thrice cites the line statements of the Qian hexagram and explains them in order to show that sagely virtue becomes manifest gradually. Now, that sagely virtue becomes manifest gradually is because it advances gradually in accordance with time and position. In the "Words of the Text" (Wenyan), when the Sage thrice cites the line statements of the Qian hexagram and expounds the meaning of each, could it be without intention? Moreover, the various lines of Qian all possess the virtue of the sage. Yet for the Nine in the Third place, the Duke of Zhou appended the words "all day long active and vigilant," and the Master further expounded this as "carrying out affairs"—why is this? It is because Nine in the Third place occupies the top of the lower trigram, being doubly yang and not in the central position. What he ought to attend to is simply advancing in virtue; therefore all day long he is anxious and diligent, carrying out the business of advancing in virtue without ceasing. What he ought to carry out is simply cultivating his enterprise; therefore all day long he is cautious and alert, carrying out the business of cultivating his enterprise without interruption. This is why it is called "carrying out affairs." Now, "carrying out affairs" is not yet manifested in practical application; only at the time of Nine in the Fourth place is it then tested. title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
公係以或躍在淵矣而夫子又申之曰自試也蓋四
當進退未定之時有龍或躍在淵之象故德已進矣
而未遽有為姑自試其德可行則行焉業已修矣而
未始有用姑自試其業可用則用焉此所以為自試
其可也夫自試猶未及於行必於九五之時而後行
焉九五之爻周公係以飛龍在天矣而夫子又申之
曰上治也蓋以九五得時得位有飛龍在天之象故
昔之所進修者今則大行於天下而無不漸被矣向
之所自試者今則大布於四海而無不覆冒矣此所
===
以為居上治下也夫三也四也五也其位以漸而尊
行事也自試也上治也則德以漸而顯吾夫子歷舉
而申之周公係爻之意不既明矣乎大抵乾之一卦
皆以聖人明之有隱顯而無淺深特内卦以德學言
外卦以時位言九四之待時備九三之學也九五之
上治出九四之時也孰謂乾乾之君子而非利見之
大人乎吁學易者宜潛心焉
六爻之動三極之道也是故君子所居而安者
易之序也所樂而玩者爻之辭也是故居則

translation_en:
…[the Duke of] Zhou appended the words "wavering over the depths," and the Master further expounded upon this by saying, "He tests himself." This is because the fourth line corresponds to a time when advancing and retreating are not yet decided, bearing the image of a dragon wavering over the depths. Therefore, although his virtue has already advanced, he does not hastily take action, instead tentatively testing his virtue and acting only if it is practicable; although his enterprise has already been cultivated, it has not yet been put to use, so he tentatively tests his enterprise and employs it only if it is usable. This is what is meant by testing what is feasible for himself. Yet testing oneself still stops short of full enactment, which occurs only at the time of the Nine in the Fifth place. For the line of Nine in the Fifth, the Duke of Zhou appended the words "the flying dragon is in the heavens," and the Master further expounded upon this by saying, "He governs from above." This is because Nine in the Fifth has attained both the right time and the right position, bearing the image of a flying dragon in the heavens. Therefore, what he formerly advanced and cultivated is now carried out on a grand scale throughout the realm, with nothing left untouched by its gradual influence; what he previously tested for himself is now broadly распространено across the four seas, with nothing left unembraced under its canopy. This is what is meant by dwelling above to govern those below. As for the third, the fourth, and the fifth lines, their positions become progressively more exalted; as for "putting into practice," "testing oneself," and "governing from above," the virtue becomes progressively more manifest. When our Master enumerated each in turn and expounded upon them, was not the meaning of the Duke of Zhou's appended line statements made thoroughly clear? On the whole, the entire hexagram of Qian is elucidated in terms of the sage: there is a difference between being hidden and being manifest, but no difference in depth or shallowness. It is simply that the inner trigram speaks in terms of virtue and learning, whereas the outer trigram speaks in terms of time and position. Nine in the Fourth's awaiting the right time is fully equipped with the learning of Nine in the Third; Nine in the Fifth's governing from above emerges from the timely readiness of Nine in the Fourth. Who would say that the tirelessly diligent superior man is not the same as the great man whom it is advantageous to see? Ah! Those who study the Changes ought to immerse their minds in this.

Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor (jiaoyu) Hou: The principle of the Three Ultimates runs through the entire topic. While candidates writing on it occasionally grasp this idea, when it comes to the quiescent and active states of the superior man's body and mind, they mostly fail to elucidate it. Only in this essay have we found a genuine personal realization and a precise exposition; the author must be someone deeply versed in this Classic.

Comment by Associate Examiner Director of Studies (xuezheng) Zhu: Those in the examination compound who wrote on this topic divided it into either three sections or two sections; when elaborate, they erred in verbosity, and when concise, they erred in obscurity, offering nothing pleasing at all. Only this essay establishes its argument around the sages making the Changes (Yi) and the superior man studying the Changes. Developing its narrative from beginning to end, it achieves perfection in both diction and principle. Superior to the other papers, it is a fine work.

Comment by Examiner Reader-in-waiting (shidu) Yin: The diction and reasoning are closely woven and meticulous; no one who is not deeply learned in studying the Changes could have produced this.

Comment by Examiner Academician (xueshi) Chen: To explain the Changes to this level may truly be called having grasped its essential purport.

The transformations of the hexagram lines embody the principles of the Three Powers (Heaven, Earth, and Man), and the superior man who studies the Changes obtains natural blessings. Indeed, because the principles of the Three Powers are embodied within the transformations of the hexagram lines, since the quiescent and active states of the superior man's body and mind do not depart from the principles of the hexagrams, how could he not obtain the blessings of Heaven! In ancient times, when the sages made the Changes, they first drew the three lines of the inner trigram and then doubled them by drawing the three lines of the outer trigram. title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
故爻之初二地也初為地之剛二為地之柔而初二
之變化一地之道焉爻之三四人也三為人之仁四
為人之義而三四之變化一人之道焉爻之五與上
非天乎五為天之陽上為天之陰是五上之變化一
天之道也六爻之動具三極之理如此苟非君子又
豈能學之乎是故易之所著無非事理當然之序君
子身之所居而安者則惟循其序焉爻之所係無非
吉凶悔吝之辭君子心之所樂而玩者則惟在其詞
焉此其身心之所契者不外乎三極之道也卦有象
===
而後有辭君子靜而學易則既觀其象而又玩辭以
考其所處之當否筮有變而後有占君子動而諏蓍
則既觀其變而又玩占以考其所值之吉凶此其動
靜之體夫易者亦不外此三極之道也是以自天降
康而動罔不吉申命自天而行無不利蓋天者理而
已矣君子體夫易即所以體夫天此其所以獲乎天
之福也歟抑觀易之為易不外乎辭變象占而已然
非聖人作易於前則辭變象占之體無由而立非君
子學易於後則辭變象占之用無由而行于以見聖

punctuated: 故爻之初、二，地也，初為地之剛，二為地之柔，而初、二之變化，一地之道焉；爻之三、四，人也，三為人之仁，四為人之義，而三、四之變化，一人之道焉；爻之五與上，非天乎？五為天之陽，上為天之陰，是五、上之變化，一天之道也。六爻之動，具三極之理如此，苟非君子，又豈能學之乎？是故《易》之所著，無非事理當然之序，君子身之所居而安者，則惟循其序焉；爻之所係，無非吉凶悔吝之辭，君子心之所樂而玩者，則惟在其詞焉。此其身心之所契者，不外乎三極之道也。卦有象而後有辭，君子靜而學《易》，則既觀其象而又玩辭，以考其所處之當否；筮有變而後有占，君子動而諏蓍，則既觀其變而又玩占，以考其所值之吉凶。此其動靜之體夫《易》者，亦不外此三極之道也。是以自天降康而動罔不吉，申命自天而行無不利。蓋天者，理而已矣。君子體夫《易》，即所以體夫天，此其所以獲乎天之福也歟！抑觀《易》之為《易》，不外乎辭、變、象、占而已。然非聖人作《易》於前，則辭、變、象、占之體無由而立；非君子學《易》於後，則辭、變、象、占之用無由而行。于以見聖
translation_en:
… Therefore, the first and second lines are Earth: the first is the firmness of Earth, the second is the softness of Earth, and the transformations of the first and second lines are wholly the Way of Earth. The third and fourth lines are Humanity: the third is the benevolence of Humanity, the fourth is the righteousness of Humanity, and the transformations of the third and fourth lines are wholly the Way of Humanity. Are not the fifth and topmost lines Heaven? The fifth is the yang of Heaven, the topmost is the yin of Heaven, so the transformations of the fifth and topmost lines are wholly the Way of Heaven. Since the movements of the six lines embody the principles of the Three Ultimates in this manner, if one is not a noble man, how could one learn from them?

Therefore, what the Book of Changes (Yi) manifests is nothing other than the proper sequence of affairs and principles, and that in which the noble man abides in person with ease is simply following this sequence; what is appended to the lines is nothing other than words of good fortune, misfortune, remorse, and regret, and that in which the noble man delights and which he contemplates in his mind lies simply in these words. Thus, that with which his person and mind are in accord is nothing outside the Way of the Three Ultimates. A hexagram has images and only afterward judgments; when the noble man is at rest and studies the Book of Changes, he both observes its images and ponders its judgments to examine whether his own conduct is fitting or not. Divination has transformations and only afterward prognostications; when the noble man is in action and consults the yarrow stalks, he both observes their transformations and ponders the prognostications to examine the good fortune or misfortune of the situation he encounters. Thus, his embodying of the Book of Changes in both action and rest is likewise nothing outside this Way of the Three Ultimates. Therefore, blessings are sent down from Heaven and in his actions nothing is not auspicious; mandates are renewed from Heaven and in his conduct nothing is not advantageous. For Heaven is simply principle. When the noble man embodies the Book of Changes, that is the very means by which he embodies Heaven—is this not why he obtains the blessings of Heaven?

Moreover, when we consider what makes the Book of Changes the Book of Changes, it is nothing outside of judgments, transformations, images, and prognostications. Yet had the sages not created the Book of Changes beforehand, the substance of judgments, transformations, images, and prognostications would have had no means to be established; and had the noble man not studied the Book of Changes afterward, the function of judgments, transformations, images, and prognostications would have had no means to be carried out. Hereby we see that the sages’…

title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
人之作易無非成天地之能君子之學易有以與天
地之能大哉聖人作易之功乎至哉君子學易之功
乎
書義
脩厥身允德協于下惟明后先王子惠困窮民
服厥命罔有不悅並其有邦厥鄰乃曰徯我
后后来無罰王懋乃德視乃烈祖無時豫怠
奉先思孝接下思恭視遠惟明聽德惟聰
俞圭
===
同考試官訓導葉 批破長題貴簡而盡而講不貴瑣屑也塲中
作此題多為所窘不冗則拘惟此作破簡講

身允德協下為一意末以孝恭聰明為懋

人之作《易》，無非成天地之能；君子之學《易》，有以與天地之能。大哉！聖人作《易》之功乎！至哉！君子學《易》之功乎！

書義
「脩厥身，允德協于下，惟明后。先王子惠困窮，民服厥命，罔有不悅。並其有邦，厥鄰乃曰：『徯我后，后来無罰。』王懋乃德，視乃烈祖，無時豫怠。奉先思孝，接下思恭，視遠惟明，聽德惟聰。」
俞圭
同考試官訓導葉批：破長題貴簡而盡，而講不貴瑣屑也。塲中作此題，多為所窘，不冗則拘。惟此作破簡講明，能發伊尹忠愛之意，使太甲聞之，能不拜手乎？
同考試官教諭王批：題雖冠冕，學者多體認不真。惟此卷講「修身允德協下」為一意，末以孝、恭、聰、明為「懋德」，仍歸之「明后」、「先王」，誠他卷所不能到。置之前列，孰曰不宜？
考試官侍讀尹批：詞意完整，當是作者。
translation_en:
… the sages' creation of the Book of Changes (Yi) is nothing other than bringing to completion the capabilities of Heaven and Earth, and the noble man's study of the Book of Changes enables him to participate in the capabilities of Heaven and Earth. Great indeed is the achievement of the sages in creating the Changes! Supreme indeed is the achievement of the noble man in studying the Changes!

Exposition on the Book of Documents (Shu yi)
"When he cultivates his person, and his sincere virtue harmonizes with those below, he is an enlightened sovereign. The former king treated the distressed and impoverished with parental kindness; the people submitted to his commands, and there were none who did not rejoice. Even among the neighboring states that simultaneously held territory, the neighbors said: 'We wait for our sovereign; when our sovereign comes, we shall suffer no punishment.' Oh King, strive in your virtue, look to your meritorious ancestor, and never indulge in ease or idleness. In serving your ancestors, think of filial piety; in receiving your subordinates, think of respect; in looking afar, seek clarity of vision; in listening to virtue, seek acuteness of hearing." [Book of Documents, "Tai Jia" II]

Yu Gui 俞圭

Associate Examiner, Assistant Instructor (Xundao) Ye comments: In breaking open (po) a long topic, one values being concise yet comprehensive, while in the exposition (jiang) one does not value triviality. In the examination hall, most who wrote on this topic were hampered by it—if they were not verbose, they were stiff. Only this essay breaks the topic concisely and expounds it clearly, bringing out Yi Yin's 伊尹 intent of loyal affection. Were Tai Jia 太甲 to hear it, how could he not bow his head to his hands?

Associate Examiner, Instructor (Jiaoyu) Wang comments: Although the topic is grand and dignified, most scholars fail to grasp its true meaning. Only this paper expounds "cultivating the person and harmonizing sincere virtue with those below" as a single continuous idea, and at the end treats filial piety, respect, acuteness of hearing, and clarity of vision as "striving in virtue," while still tying them back to the "enlightened sovereign" and the "former king." This is truly something other papers could not achieve. Placing it in the forefront—who would say it is inappropriate?

Examiner, Expositor-in-waiting (Shidu) Yin comments: The phrasing and meaning are complete and well-rounded; he must be an accomplished writer.

title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
考試官學士陳　批〔理能得旨詞不襲陳可取〕
大臣期君以脩身之効而徵諸先王所已然勉君以
法祖之功而詳夫事為所當然蓋修身而使實德孚
於民者明君之能事先王所已然也後王欲法先王
之勉德可不隨事致思而盡其所當然哉昔伊尹敬
復太甲之意若曰人君一身萬化之原其可以不修
乎是故檢身不可無法度也必省察吾身不以欲敗
度使實德孚契于人心可也治身不可無禮儀也必
克治吾身不以縱敗禮使實德協和于民心可也身
===
修德誠而協下如此豈庸君暗主所可能必既明且
哲之君斯能爾也然古之明君孰有過于先王成湯
乎先王於困窮之民也愛之如子而一出於誠心故
近而商邑之民也服其命今無不咸得其歡心不但
近者悅而已遠而鄰國諸侯之民亦皆仰之以為君
而曰待我君父矣我君來其必除其邪虐而出我於
水火乎伐虐以寬而拯我於塗炭乎先王之德協于
下如此今王可不法先王之德乎彼日新又新先王
所以懋昭大德也王之懋德必視法先王而不使有
alt_text:
考試官學士陳　批理俱得旨詞不憚博可取
大臣期君以脩身之效而徵諸先王所已然勉君以
法祖之功而詳夫事爲所當然蓋脩身而使實德孚
於民者明君之能事先王所已然也後王欲法先王
之勉德可不隨事致思而盡其所當然哉昔伊尹敬
複太甲之意若曰人君一身萬化之原其可以不脩
乎是故檢身不可無法度也必省察吾身不以欲敗
度使實德孚契于人心可也治身不可無禮儀也必
克治吾身不以縱敗禮使實德協和于民心可也身
===
脩德誠而協下如此豈庸君暗主所可能必既明且
哲之君斯能爾也然古之明君孰有過于先王成湯
乎先王於困窮之民也愛之如子而一出於誠心故
近而商邑之民也服其命令無不咸得其懽心不但
近者悅而已遠而鄰國諸侯之民亦皆仰之以爲君
而曰待我君久矣我君來其必除其邪虐而出我於
水火乎代虐以寬而拯我於塗炭乎先王之德協于
下如此今王可不法先王之德乎彼日新又新先王
所以懋昭大德也王之懋德必視法先王而不使有
punctuated:
考試官學士陳批：〔理能得旨，詞不襲陳，可取。〕

大臣期君以脩身之効，而徵諸先王所已然；勉君以法祖之功，而詳夫事為所當然。蓋修身而使實德孚於民者，明君之能事，先王所已然也。後王欲法先王之勉德，可不隨事致思而盡其所當然哉？昔伊尹敬復太甲之意，若曰：人君一身，萬化之原，其可以不修乎？是故檢身不可無法度也，必省察吾身，不以欲敗度，使實德孚契于人心可也；治身不可無禮儀也，必克治吾身，不以縱敗禮，使實德協和于民心可也。身修德誠而協下如此，豈庸君暗主所可能？必既明且哲之君斯能爾也。然古之明君，孰有過于先王成湯乎？先王於困窮之民也，愛之如子，而一出於誠心；故近而商邑之民也，服其命今，無不咸得其歡心。不但近者悅而已，遠而鄰國諸侯之民，亦皆仰之以為君，而曰：「待我君父矣！我君來，其必除其邪虐，而出我於水火乎？伐虐以寬，而拯我於塗炭乎？」先王之德協于下如此，今王可不法先王之德乎？彼日新又新，先王所以懋昭大德也；王之懋德，必視法先王，而不使有…
translation_en:
Examiner and Academician Chen's comment: [Its reasoning grasps the main point, and its phrasing does not copy stale clichés; it is acceptable.]

The great minister expects from his ruler the efficacy of personal cultivation, verifying it through what the Former King had already accomplished; he urges his ruler toward the achievement of emulating his ancestor, detailing what ought to be done in every affair. For to cultivate one's person and cause genuine virtue to inspire confidence in the people is the capability of an enlightened ruler, and what the Former King had already accomplished. When a successor king wishes to emulate the Former King's diligent cultivation of virtue, how could he not direct his thoughts to every affair and fulfill what ought to be done?

In antiquity, when Yi Yin reverently restored the government to Tai Jia, his meaning was as if to say: The ruler's own person is the source of myriad transformations—how could it not be cultivated? Therefore, in restraining oneself one cannot be without laws and measures: one must examine oneself, not ruining measures through desires, so as to make genuine virtue inspire confidence and accord with human hearts. In governing oneself one cannot be without ritual and decorum: one must master oneself, not ruining ritual through indulgence, so as to make genuine virtue harmonize with the minds of the people. Cultivating one's person, making one's virtue sincere, and harmonizing with those below in such a manner—how could this be within the capability of a mediocre ruler or a benighted lord? Only a ruler who is both enlightened and wise is capable of this.

Yet among the enlightened rulers of antiquity, who surpassed the Former King Cheng Tang? Toward the distressed and impoverished people, the Former King loved them as his own children, and everything issued from a sincere heart. Therefore, near at hand, the people of the capital city of Shang submitted to his commands and orders [? 命今, for 命令], and there were none whose joyful hearts were not won over. And not only were those near at hand pleased; far away, the people of the feudal lords of neighboring states also all looked up to him as their ruler, saying: "We have waited for our sovereign and father! When our sovereign comes, will he not surely eradicate their wicked tyranny and deliver us from flood and fire? Will he not punish tyranny with寬 (magnanimity) and rescue us from mire and charcoal?"

The Former King's virtue harmonized with those below like this—how could Your Majesty today not emulate the Former King's virtue? That daily renewal and ever-continuing renewal was whereby the Former King diligently made bright his great virtue; in Your Majesty's diligent cultivation of virtue, you must look to and emulate the Former King, and not allow there to be…

title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
須臾之佚豫可也昧爽丕顯先王所以顧諟明命也
王之勉德必觀法先王而不使有頃刻之怠惰可也
然亦何所當從事乎夫德不外乎孝恭必也奉先思
孝接下思恭焉思孝則不敢違於祖思恭則不敢忽
於臣德不外乎聰明必也視遠惟明聽德惟聰焉惟
明則不蔽於淺近惟聰則不惑於憸邪王能懋德如
此則德豈有不合於先王而不足為明君哉抑觀當
太甲不惠阿衡之時伊尹之言惟恐太甲不聽及太
甲改過之後太甲之心惟恐伊尹不言是以此篇上
===
文太甲既拜稽而以圖終之道責之伊尹至此尹復
拜稽而以明君之事望之太甲君臣相責望如此此
太甲所以為商令王伊尹所以為商賢佐也歟
萬年厭于乃德殷乃引考王伻殷乃承叙萬年
吳寔

同考試官教諭王 批〔本房書經餘六百卷窘於此題者比比〕

拜稽而以圖終之道責之伊尹至此尹復
拜稽而以明君之事望之太甲君臣相責望如此此
太甲所以爲商令王伊尹所以爲商賢佐也歟

□□
同考試官訓導□□　批此題本祈天永命而作者多串說聞
知之文說厭飽乃德之旨殊無定見此作一出
群疑破矣
同考試官教諭王　批本房書經餘六百卷看於此題者比比
punctuated:
須臾之佚豫可也。昧爽丕顯，先王所以顧諟明命也；王之勉德，必觀法先王，而不使有頃刻之怠惰可也。然亦何所當從事乎？夫德不外乎孝恭，必也「奉先思孝，接下思恭」焉；思孝則不敢違於祖，思恭則不敢忽於臣。德不外乎聰明，必也「視遠惟明，聽德惟聰」焉；惟明則不蔽於淺近，惟聰則不惑於憸邪。王能懋德如此，則德豈有不合於先王，而不足為明君哉！抑觀當太甲不惠阿衡之時，伊尹之言惟恐太甲不聽；及太甲改過之後，太甲之心惟恐伊尹不言。是以此篇上文，太甲既拜稽而以圖終之道責之伊尹，至此，尹復拜稽而以明君之事望之太甲。君臣相責望如此，此太甲所以為商令王，伊尹所以為商賢佐也歟！

萬年厭于乃德，殷乃引考；王伻殷乃承叙萬年。
吳寔
同考試官訓導葉批：〔此題本祈禱、責難兩意，而作者多串說。間知之，又詭「厭飽乃德」之旨，殊無定見。此作一出，群疑破矣。〕
同考試官教諭王批：〔本房《書經》餘六百卷，窘於此題者比比。〕
translation_en:
… a single moment of idle pleasure. At dawn he displayed his great virtue—this was how the Former King kept his eyes ever upon the bright mandate of Heaven; in exerting himself in virtue, the King must observe and model himself upon the Former King, and must not allow himself a single instant of indolence. Yet what specifically ought he to apply himself to? Now, virtue is nothing other than filial piety and reverence: he must, "in serving his ancestors, think of filial piety, and in receiving his subordinates, think of reverence." Thinking of filial piety, he will not dare transgress against his ancestors; thinking of reverence, he will not dare slight his ministers. Virtue is nothing other than acute hearing and clear sight: he must, "in looking afar, seek clear sight, and in listening to virtue, seek acute hearing." With clear sight, he will not be blinded by what is shallow and near at hand; with acute hearing, he will not be deluded by flatterers and evil men. If the King can exert himself in virtue like this, how could his virtue fail to match that of the Former King, and how could he fall short of being an enlightened ruler? Moreover, consider that when Tai Jia did not heed the Yin [Aheng], Yi Yin spoke out only fearing that Tai Jia would not listen; yet after Tai Jia reformed his faults, Tai Jia in his heart only feared that Yi Yin would not speak. Therefore, earlier in this chapter, after Tai Jia bowed and knocked his head to the ground, charging Yi Yin with the way to plan for the end, at this point Yi Yin in turn bowed and knocked his head to the ground, placing his hopes in Tai Jia to carry out the work of an enlightened ruler. Ruler and minister charged and placed such hopes in one another—is this not why Tai Jia became an exemplary king of Shang, and why Yi Yin became a worthy minister of Shang?

"For ten thousand years they will beimbued with your virtue, and Yin will enjoy prolonged prosperity; the King will cause Yin to succeed to the regular order for ten thousand years."
By Wu Shi 吳寔.
Comment by Associate Examiner Assistant Instructor Ye: [This topic originally contains two distinct ideas—prayer to the ancestors and urging difficult duties upon the king—yet most candidates conflated them into a single continuous argument. Those few who recognized the distinction distorted the meaning of "satisfied with your virtue" (yan bao nai de), showing no settled view at all. Once this essay appeared, all doubts were dispelled.]

title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
晚得此卷上以為周公致禱先王下以為
責難成王破既典雅而講亦勻稱誠璧經中
巨擘也録之以示後來
考試官侍讀尹批發揚周公忠愛之意藹然可見
考試官學士陳批作是篇者多戾旨此作得之而詞足以達
佳製也
大臣致禱前王以垂德澤於無間責難後王以致治
化於無窮盖德澤被于子孫殷民者此大臣所以為
君禱也而欲君化服殷民於萬年又非大臣所以責
===
難於君乎周公為國家長遠之慮盖如此昔周公不
敢當成王命寧之禮而以祭于文武遂為成王禱故
當使歸之日述其祭祝之辭若謂昔汝文武之創業
固欲傳之於萬年不但傳之成王而止也今汝於昭
於天可不默相之乎要必永錫祚胤使億萬斯年本
支百世者皆得厭飽乃德而穆穆皇皇宜君宜王也
昔汝文武之受民固欲躋之於壽域不徒澤及一時
而已也今爾在帝左右可不陰佑之乎要必相協厥
居使侯服我周膚敏裸將者亦得各全性命而資富

translation_en:
… Late in the grading I obtained this paper: the first part takes it as the Duke of Zhou offering prayers to the former kings, and the second part takes it as his urging difficult duties upon King Cheng. Its opening statement of the theme is classic and refined, and its exposition is also well-balanced. Truly it is a masterpiece among the essays on the Classic of History (璧經); I record it to serve as a model for future students.

Examiner Academician Reader-in-Waiting Yin comments: It brings out the Duke of Zhou's loyal and affectionate intent, which is warmly visible.

Examiner Academician Chen comments: Those who wrote on this topic mostly missed the purport. This composition grasps it, and its language suffices to convey it—a fine piece of work.

The great minister offers prayers to the former kings so as to hand down the blessings of their virtue without interruption, and urges difficult duties upon the successor king so as to bring about transformative governance without end. Indeed, that the blessings of virtue should reach both his descendants and the people of Yin—this is why the great minister prays on behalf of his ruler; and desiring that the ruler transform and bring the people of Yin into submission for ten thousand years—is this not in turn why the great minister urges difficult duties upon his ruler? Such were the Duke of Zhou's far-reaching concerns for the dynasty.

In the past, the Duke of Zhou did not dare to accept for himself the gifts of King Cheng's mission of pacification and inquiry, and instead used them to sacrifice to Kings Wen and Wu, thereupon praying on King Cheng's behalf. Thus, on the day he sent the messenger back, he recounted the words of his sacrificial prayer, as if to say: In the past, when you, Wen and Wu, founded the dynastic enterprise, you surely wished to transmit it for ten thousand years, and not merely stop with transmitting it to King Cheng. Now that you shine brightly in Heaven, how could you not silently aid him? You must forever bestow blessings and posterity, so that for myriads of years, the main line and collateral branches for a hundred generations may all beimbued and satisfied with your virtue, majestic and august, fit to be rulers and fit to be kings. In the past, when you, Wen and Wu, received the people, you surely wished to raise them into the realm of longevity, and not merely extend your blessings to a single age. Now that you are at the left and right of the Supreme Lord, how could you not secretly protect them? You must assist in harmonizing their dwellings, so that those who submit as feudatories to our Zhou, admirable and swift in assisting at the libation sacrifices, may also each preserve their lives in full, and through wealth become…

title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
能訓惟以永年也周公既述祭祝之辭以復成王矣
而又致夫責難之意焉盖謂誕保受民王嘗命予旦
矣然化殷之本得不在於王身乎王必于棐民彝次
第其教條使以蕩陵德者莫不承服我周之教條而
式化厥訓萬年猶一日也承保受民我固嘗許王矣
然治化之原有不係於王躬乎王必繼天立極序秩
其教令使怙侈滅義者莫不聽受我周之教令而臣
服多遜萬載如一時也是則始而曰萬年禱于文武
之意深終而曰萬年期諸成王之意遠自非周公之
===
忠愛其孰能與於此哉雖然周公致禱於先王責難
於成王若自諉矣殊不知殷民未服王業未安周公
幽則祈之神明則望之君忠誠迫切自不容已於言
也異時殷民允升大猷有周歷年八百謂非周公輔
導之力可乎
詩義
豈曰無衣與子同袍王于興師修我戈矛與子
同仇豈曰無衣與子同澤王于興師修我矛
戟與子偕作豈曰無衣與子同裳王于興師

translation_en:
… and able to be instructed, so that they may enjoy longevity. Having related the words of the sacrificial prayer in reply to King Cheng, the Duke of Zhou then conveyed the meaning of urging difficult duties upon his sovereign. For he meant to say: "Greatly to protect the people received from Heaven is what Your Majesty once commanded me, Dan; yet does not the root of transforming Yin lie in Your Majesty's own person? Your Majesty must aid the constant nature of the people and set forth in order the articles of instruction, so that those who in dissipation transgress against virtue will all submit to the articles of instruction of our Zhou and be transformed by those teachings, for ten thousand years as if a single day. To uphold and protect the people received from Heaven is indeed what I once promised Your Majesty; yet is not the source of governing and transforming bound up with Your Majesty's own person? Your Majesty must succeed Heaven in establishing the standard of perfection and arrange in order the ordinances of instruction, so that those who rely on extravagance to destroy righteousness will all heed and receive the ordinances of instruction of our Zhou, submitting as subjects in great humility, for ten thousand ages as if a single moment." Thus, when he first speaks of "ten thousand years," the intention of his prayer to Kings Wen and Wu is profound; when at the end he speaks of "ten thousand years," the expectation he places upon King Cheng is far-reaching. Were it not for the loyalty and devotion of the Duke of Zhou, who could be capable of this? Even so, in offering prayers to the former kings and urging difficult duties upon King Cheng, it might seem as though the Duke of Zhou were shifting the responsibility from himself. Yet little does one realize that when the people of Yin were not yet submissive and the royal enterprise was not yet secure, in the unseen realm the Duke of Zhou prayed to the spirits, and in the visible realm he placed his hopes in his ruler—his loyalty and sincerity were so urgent that he could not help speaking thus. When in later times the people of Yin truly rose to the great Way and the House of Zhou endured for eight hundred years, could one say that this was not through the power of the Duke of Zhou's guidance and assistance?

Exposition on the Classic of Poetry (Shijing)

"How shall it be said that you have no clothes? I will share my long robes with you. The king is raising his forces; I will prepare my lance and spear, and share the same foe with you. How shall it be said that you have no clothes? I will share my undergarments with you. The king is raising his forces; I will prepare my spear and halberd, and rise up together with you. How shall it be said that you have no clothes? I will share my lower garments with you. The king is raising his forces, …"

… I will prepare my armor and weapons, and march off together with you."

Deng Cunde 鄧存德

Associate Examiner and Instructor Xu 徐 comments: This topic originally speaks of how the people of Qin were able to rush to the call of duty, thereby showing the beauty of Qin customs. Most writers take the opposite view, and when explaining "no clothes" their treatment is mostly blunt and flat, utterly lacking in flavor. Coming suddenly upon this essay, with its gentle, flowing language and calm, unhurried spirit, it brings out the feelings of mutual bonding and mutual commitment among the people of Qin right before one's eyes; and his other essays are also detailed, refined, and worth reading. Among the Classic of Poetry (Shijing) papers, this scroll should be ranked first.

Associate Examiner and Instructor Luo 羅 comments: The Classic of Poetry scrolls number no fewer than eight hundred and more, yet most writers are unable to portray the nuances and fully express the poet's meaning, making them quite unworthy of note. This piece enters sympathetically into the topic and its writing develops the ideas well; it is an outstanding work from this examination ward.

Examiner and Academician Reader-in-Waiting Yin 尹 comments: By focusing on the admirable aspects of Qin customs, he captures the spirit of gentle and sincere moderation (wenrou dunhou). He must be a fine scholar.

Examiner and Academician Chen 陳 comments: This scroll completely washes away stale clichés and shines with an extraordinary, spirited vigor—indeed, it is not merely this single essay that is excellent.

The poet shares the garments he possesses, so that the bond of affection grows ever closer; he keeps in mind the duty of following the king, so that the mutual pledge of heroic spirit reaches the utmost degree. Indeed, in sharing the long robe, sharing the undergarment, and sharing the lower garment, one can see the closeness of their bond; in sharing the same enemy, rising up together, and marching off together, one sees even more the depth of their mutual commitment. Yet they are also able not to forget the duty of following the king—is this custom of the people of Qin not still imbued with the surviving ethos of the Western Zhou? In olden times, the customs of Qin were fierce and brave, delighting in battle; therefore, in days of leisure, through affection…

title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
相結而相謂曰我豈以子之無衣而思與子同袍乎
袍乃枲著之所成賤者之常服爾今與子而同之所
以冀爾志之吾合也他日倘有王者之命興戡亂之
師則將脩我之戈矛敵王之所愾實欲與子同仇而
毋舍焉同袍之恩至親矣然猶未也故又曰我豈以
子之無衣而願與子同澤乎澤乃近膚之所服垢澤
之微衣爾今與子而共之所以望爾情之吾洽也他
日脫承天王之命舉禦侮之旅則又將整我之戈戟
揚國之威武實欲與子偕作而弗忘焉同澤之情亦
===
已篤矣猶未已也故復相謂曰我豈謂子之無衣而
與子同裳乎裳實下體之衣亦衣之賤者爾然裳服
之是同則恩義之愈密又擬肅將乎天威脩飾乎甲
兵一有所征伐也固欲與子偕行而不蹔違矣吁秦

藹然溢於言表何其俗之勇於義哉抑考之當是時
也國有大耻而莫知爲之雪王有大讎而莫知爲之
復可見諸侯無意於王室也至矣而秦人毅然以天

translation_en: … bound themselves together, saying to one another: "Is it really because you have no clothes that I think of sharing my padded robe with you? A padded robe is made with hemp batting, merely the everyday garment of a humble man. In sharing it with you now, I hope that your resolve will unite with mine. Someday, should there be a command from the true King raising an army to quell disorder, I shall ready my dagger-axe and spear to oppose the object of the King's wrath, truly wishing to face the same foe alongside you without ever forsaking you." The bond of sharing a padded robe is most intimate indeed, yet even that is not all. Thus they say again: "Is it really because you have no clothes that I wish to share my undershirt with you? An undershirt is worn next to the skin, merely a lowly garment that catches sweat and grime. In sharing it with you now, I hope that your feelings will harmonize with mine. Someday, should we receive the command of the Heavenly King mobilizing troops to repel insult, I shall once again put in order my dagger-axe and halberd to display the state's martial might, truly wishing to rise up together with you and never forget our bond." The sentiment of sharing an undershirt is already deep indeed, yet still it does not stop there. Thus they say to one another once more: "Do I really say you have no clothes, and so share my lower garment with you? A lower garment is in truth clothing for the lower body, also a humble sort of dress. Yet when even lower garments are shared, the bond of affection and duty grows tighter still. And intending reverently to carry out the heavenly majesty and to make ready our armor and weapons, as soon as a punitive expedition is launched, I certainly wish to march alongside you without parting even for a moment." Ah! Within a single poem, the people of Qin use repeated words to convey an earnest, reiterated meaning; mutual affection and high-spirited camaraderie overflow warmly beyond the words themselves—how brave in righteousness were their customs! Moreover, if we examine that era: the state had suffered a great disgrace, yet none knew to wipe it away; the King had a great enemy, yet none knew to avenge him. From this one can see to what extreme the feudal lords had lost all concern for the royal house. punctuated:
於耕種之際，人力齊而饁餉勤，苗生盛而收成富，則稼穡之事，非惟此處而有之也。穫羙利而至萬億及秭之多，為酒醴而供以洽百禮之用，燕賓而為邦家之光，養老而致胡考之寧，則豐年之慶，非獨今時而得之也。盖自我周家開國以來，皆以務農為本。遡文、武而上及於太王，所傳非一世也，而此稼穡之事，如茨如梁，已無一處而不如此矣，豈但今時而已哉？推公劉而上至於后稷，所歷非一君也，而此豐年之慶，自天降康，已無一時而不若是矣，又豈徒今日而已哉？謂之「振古如兹」，信乎所從來者遠也。吁！言農功之盛，則曰「非自我始」；推田事之來，則曰「率由古先」。周家忠厚之意，一詠歌間未嘗舍置，先王德澤之深，寧不於斯而可見乎？不特此也，觀其歷序夫墾闢播種之勤，詳述夫饁餉耘治之悉，與夫烝畀祖妣、燕賓養老，無不周至，讀之者宛然想見盛時太平氣象，《載芟》詩人可謂善於詠歌者矣。

《春秋》義
王人子突救衛〔莊公六年〕、齊人救邢〔閔公元年〕、晉趙盾帥…
translation_en:
…at the time of plowing and planting, when human labor is united and the delivery of field rations is diligent, when the sprouts grow luxuriantly and the harvest is abundant—then the business of sowing and reaping is not found in this place alone. When the fine profit of the harvest reaches tens of thousands, hundreds of millions, and billions, when spirits and sweet wine are made and offered to fulfill the needs of the hundred rites, when guests are feasted to bring glory to the state and family, and when the elderly are nourished to bring peace to those of advanced age—then the blessing of a bountiful year is not obtained in the present time alone. For ever since our House of Zhou founded the state, all have taken devotion to agriculture as the root. Tracing back from Kings Wen and Wu up to King Tai, what was transmitted was not of a single generation; and in this business of sowing and reaping, with grain stacked like thatch and like bridges, there was already no place where it was not like this—how could it be only at the present time? Tracing back from Duke Liu up to Hou Ji, those who succeeded one another were not a single ruler; and in this blessing of a bountiful year, with peace sent down from Heaven, there was already no time when it was not like this—how, again, could it be merely today? When the ode calls it "from of old, thus," truly its origins are distant indeed! Ah! In speaking of the flourishing of agricultural work, one says it did not begin with oneself; in tracing the origin of fieldwork, one says it follows the ancient predecessors. The loyal and generous spirit of the House of Zhou was never set aside even in the space of a single song; how could the depth of the former kings' virtuous bounty not be seen right here? And not only this: when one observes how the ode successively recounts the diligence of clearing land and sowing seed, describes in full detail the delivery of rations and weeding, and extends comprehensively to presenting offerings to ancestors and ancestresses, feasting guests, and nourishing the aged—those who read it can vividly imagine the peaceful and prosperous atmosphere of a flourishing age. The poet of "Clearing the Grass" (Zai shan) may truly be called skillful at singing praise!
