Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Chen: "His seven essays were composed in a single seamless breath. This essay sets up its argument around the relief of distress by the royal house and by the hegemons, which is truly right. Moreover, where the topic is brief he expands it to make it full, and where it is long he condenses it to make it concise, showing none of the rigid, mechanical habits of one who notches a boat or glues the tuning pegs. To produce such an extraordinary piece under the windswept eaves in a brief measure of time leaves all the other papers in this examination ward far behind."

Comment by Examiner Academician Reader-in-waiting Yin: "Whenever the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) records 'rescue,' it is always an expression of praise. This piece has grasped this, and since his other essays are all fine as well, he should be placed in the front ranks."

Comment by Examiner Academician Chen: "On the topic of relieving distress, judgments of praise and blame have been varied and confused, without any settled view; with this essay, the argument is finally settled."

When the royal house relieved distress in order to punish the unrighteous, the Spring and Autumn Annals recorded it with a special brush to make manifest its goodness; when the hegemonic states relieved distress in order to repel foreign barbarians, the Spring and Autumn Annals recorded it repeatedly to make manifest their admirable conduct. From this we can see that although the Spring and Autumn Annals is the same in recording "rescue," the principles it establishes therein are different. Why is this so? Executing the rebellious and punishing usurpers is the law of the Nine Punitive Expeditions. In an age when the feudal lords were abetting disorder, who was able to carry out this duty?Fortunately, King Zhuang had insight into this. At the time when the five states raised armies to attack Wei, he thereupon commanded Zitu to undertake the campaign to rescue Wei, delivering Qianmou from peril in a season when the various states were banding together in support of usurpation, and exposing the wickedness of Shuo of Wei on the day when he framed and ruined his own natural kin. Even though it did not achieve success in Wei, it was nevertheless sufficient to uphold the cardinal principles of human relations among unsubmissive states; …

…and although it may have been of no help to Mou, it was nevertheless sufficient to extend the royal mandate to an afflicted state. This is the supreme excellence in the entire Classic. How could the Spring and Autumn Annals not approve of it? Therefore, although Zitu held the humble rank of a lower serviceman, by special exception he was accorded the precedent of a grand夫 (Grand Master) and recorded by his style name. How great was its approval of his relieving distress in order to punish the unjust!

As for pacifying the Hua-Xia states and repelling the barbarians, this is the duty of a hegemon. At a time when foreign barbarians were repeatedly expanding their power, who was able to launch such campaigns? Fortunately, the hegemonic states set their resolve upon this. When Xing suffered the calamity of the Di, Duke Huan of Qi upheld righteousness and rescued it; and because the Viscount of Chu invaded Chen, Jin commanded Zhao Dun to again lead an army to rescue Chen. When Zheng suffered affliction from Chu, Xi Que raised troops to rescue it; and shortly thereafter, when Chu again attacked Zheng, Jin once more dispatched Luan Shu to mobilize an army to relieve Zheng. The righteousness of sharing disaster and rescuing those in urgent need was repeatedly manifested near and far; the merit of pacifying the Hua-Xia and repelling the barbarians was frequently seen one after another. Extinguishing the fierce flames of the people of Chu just as they were spreading, and relieving the states from their desperate plight when they were nearly in ruin—this was the proper use of military force. How could the Spring and Autumn Annals not praise it? Therefore, regarding the affairs of Qi and Jin relieving distress, it repeatedly recorded them as "rescues" without deletion. How great was its approval of their relieving distress in order to repel the barbarians!

In general, Qi and Jin relieving distress may certainly be approved, whereas Zitu's rescue of Wei alone cannot be free from criticism. For although he received the royal mandate, he returned without achievement. In the end, this resulted in Shuo of Wei finally entering the state and Qianmou finally losing his throne, while the decrees and commands of the royal house were no longer carried out in the realm, and the feudal lords' partisanship with evil grew daily more rampant among the states. Reading the Classic to this point, one cannot help closing the scroll with a sigh.

之會甫畢而再鄄之好禮復臨勤勤不已以謀國是
孜孜不倦以收人心齊桓之圖伯可謂慎矣人心感
慕安得而不從乎未幾齊仗尊周之義而講于幽之
盟宋公在列固其宜也而疑貳之魯莊亦莫不雲集
於載書之側陳侯與會固其所也而反覆之鄭伯亦
靡不雷同於牲歃之頃人心之同如此非由齊桓講
好之慎何以致此故曰伯主慎以講好而致人心之
同者此也若夫魯僖自即位以來無日不以修德為
務當夫旱暵之際由冬徂春而雨澤之不施僖也不
===
事雩禱而惟以天災為懼由春及夏而雲霓徒仰僖
也不遑他務而惟以民隱為恤心在於務農故其憂
之也深志在於省己故其閔之也至僖之閔雨可謂
勤矣天心仁愛豈有不答之耶故當六月之時而有
甘雨之應昔之枯槁者賴之而實函斯活矣向之荒
蕪者賴之而驛驛其達矣天心之應如此非魯僖閔
雨之勤曷以臻茲故曰望國勤以閔雨而感天心之
應者此也抑考齊桓慎以感人心固可予矣然後日
緣陵城而王禁犯于淮會而王爵紊獨不可譏乎魯

… assembly at Juan had barely ended when the amicable rites of the second meeting at Juan arrived in turn. Diligently and unceasingly, he planned state policies; tirelessly and assiduously, he won over the hearts of the people. Duke Huan of Qi's pursuit of hegemony can truly be called cautious! Moved to admiration, how could the hearts of the people fail to follow him? Before long, Qi upheld the righteous cause of honoring the Zhou royal house and conducted the covenant at You. That the Duke of Song was in attendance was naturally fitting; yet even the doubtful and vacillating Duke Zhuang of Lu gathered like clouds beside the covenant text. That the Marquis of Chen participated in the assembly was naturally his place; yet even the capricious Earl of Zheng echoed in unison at the moment of sacrificing the victim and smearing its blood on the lips. Such was the unity of human hearts—if not for Duke Huan of Qi's cautiousness in cultivating amity, how could this have been brought about? Therefore, when it is said that "the hegemon was cautious in cultivating amity and thus caused the hearts of the people to unite of their own accord," this is what is meant.

As for Duke Xi of Lu, ever since he ascended the throne, there was not a single day he did not make cultivating virtue his task. At a time of parching drought, from winter into spring the moisture of rain was not bestowed; yet Xi did not busy himself with rain-making sacrifices and prayers, only standing in awe of the heavenly disaster. From spring into summer, people gazed up in vain for clouds and rainbows; yet Xi had no leisure for other affairs, only feeling compassion for the sufferings of the common folk. Because his mind was set on promoting agriculture, his worry over it was deep; because his will was set on self-examination, his anxiety over it was utmost. Xi's anxiety for rain can truly be called diligent! Since the mind of Heaven is benevolent and loving, how could it fail to respond to him? Thus, in the sixth month, there was the response of timely, sweet rain. What had previously been withered relied on it so that the seeds within the husks came to life; what had hitherto lain barren relied on it so that the shoots sprouted thick and fast. Such was the response of the mind of Heaven—if not for Duke Xi of Lu's diligence in worrying over rain, how could this have been attained? Therefore, when it is said that "the prestigious state was diligent in its anxiety for rain and thus moved the mind of Heaven to respond of its own accord," this is what is meant.

Yet if we examine the matter further: that Duke Huan of Qi was cautious and thus moved the hearts of the people is certainly worthy of praise; but when on a later day he walled Yuanling and thereby violated the royal prohibitions, and assembled at Huai and thereby threw the royal ranks of nobility into disorder, can he alone escape criticism? title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
多寡必視三公焉盖三公饔餼九牢而五嶽之祭牲
亦九也三公十有六豆而五嶽之祭豆亦十有六也
以五嶽而視三公則禮之豐儉適乎中也可𥙿矣天
下之川莫大於四瀆曰江曰河曰淮曰濟是也天子
祭之其禮亦何所視乎彼諸侯維藩維垣固有功於
民而四瀆則寶貨所殖亦有利於民也故牲器之多
寡必視諸侯焉盖諸侯饔餼七牢而四瀆之祭牲亦
七也諸侯十有二豆而四瀆之祭豆亦十有二也以
四瀆而視諸侯則禮之厚薄得其中也可見矣吁明
===
而享三公即幽而祭五嶽之禮幽而祀四瀆即明而
待諸侯之禮因人神之尊卑為禮數之隆殺先王制
禮豈苟焉而已哉抑考上文既曰天子祭天地諸侯
祭社稷天子祭天下名山大川以及此矣而下文又
曰諸侯祭名山大川豈諸侯得同天子之所祭乎盖
天地有域之最大者天子則域中之所尊其所報者
衆故祭天地及名山大川之在天下者也若諸侯則
守土之臣其所報者寡故祭社稷及名山大川之在
其境者也吁祭雖報本反始之禮然上可以兼下下

For the cooked and raw food gifts for the Three Dukes consist of nine sets of sacrificial animals (lao), and the sacrificial victims for the Five Sacred Peaks (Wuyue) are likewise nine; the Three Dukes are accorded sixteen wooden offering-stands (dou), and the sacrificial offering-stands for the Five Sacred Peaks are likewise sixteen. When the Son of Heaven sacrifices to them, what is the ritual placed on a par with? Since the feudal lords (zhuhou) serve as bulwarks and walls, they certainly perform meritorious service for the people, while the Four Great Rivers are where precious goods are bred, likewise bringing benefit to the people; therefore, the quantity of sacrificial victims and vessels must be on a par with those for the feudal lords. For the cooked and raw food gifts for the feudal lords consist of seven sets of sacrificial animals, and the sacrificial victims for the Four Great Rivers are likewise seven; the feudal lords are accorded twelve wooden offering-stands, and the sacrificial offering-stands for the Four Great Rivers are likewise twelve. That placing the Four Great Rivers on a par with the feudal lords attains the proper mean between generosity and meagerness in ritual can thus be seen. Ah! In the visible realm, the ritual of feasting the Three Dukes is the very ritual used in the unseen realm to sacrifice to the Five Sacred Peaks; in the unseen realm, the ritual of sacrificing to the Four Great Rivers is the very ritual used in the visible realm to treat the feudal lords. How could the feudal lords be permitted to share in what the Son of Heaven sacrifices to? text:
不得以兼上名分所由判也禮嚴矣哉
邇臣守和宰正百官大臣慮四方
陳謨

為輔德之本先儒張子嘗曰近臣守和和其心以
脩頗對不可徇其喜怒好惡與本題方氏註
合而場中作者多惑於應氏先君德之言誤為
守君德之和亦非應氏初意問不戾旨又欠發明
獨此篇組織傳註成文足祛羣惑宜冠本房
===
考試官侍讀尹批此義融會集註意完語足傳訛襲疑者觀
之得不釋然乎
考試官學士陳批經註貴貫通執一者泥而多鑿此篇脫然於
羣課中而獨立不倚者乎
命於君者異其名盡於己者有其序蓋自邇臣以至
大臣皆命於君者也命於君者其名雖異然先君德
而後朝廷而後天下者又豈非己職之所當盡哉表記君子記此謂夫人臣居其位必思盡其職位既不
同職亦有異是故旦夕承弼左右納誨此邇臣也邇

同考試官訓導朱批：「邇臣守和」一句，本言近臣職在輔德，當守己和以為輔德之本。先儒張子嘗曰：「近臣守和，和其心以脩頗對，不可徇其喜怒好惡。」與本題方氏註合。而場中作者多惑於應氏「先君德」之言，誤為守君德之和，亦非應氏初意；間不戾旨，又欠發明。獨此篇組織傳註成文，足祛羣惑，宜冠本房。

"Attendant ministers maintain harmony; the Prime Minister rectifies the hundred officials; great ministers take thought for the four quarters."
Chen Mo 陳謨
Associate Examiner, Assistant Instructor Zhu comments: The line "Attendant ministers maintain harmony" originally means that the duty of close ministers lies in assisting the sovereign's virtue, and they should maintain their own harmony as the foundation for assisting in virtue. The former Confucian scholar Master Zhang (Zhang Zai 張載) once said: "Close ministers maintain harmony—harmonizing their minds to cultivate balanced responses [? 脩頗對, for 備顧問], and must not indulge their own joy, anger, likes, or dislikes." This accords with Mr. Fang's (Fang Que 方慤) commentary on the present passage. Yet candidates in the examination hall were mostly misled by Mr. Ying's (Ying Yong 應鏞) remark on "putting the sovereign's virtue first," mistakenly taking it to mean maintaining the harmony of the sovereign's virtue, which was not Mr. Ying's original intent either; even when occasionally they did not violate the purport, they lacked elucidation. Only this essay weaves together the commentaries to form its text, sufficing to dispel the confusion of the crowd; it deserves to top this examination ward.
Examiner, Reader-in-waiting Yin comments: This exposition thoroughly integrates the Collected Commentaries (Jizhu); its meaning is complete and its phrasing sufficient. Should those who pass on errors and inherit doubts read it, how could they not find their doubts dispelled?
Examiner, Academician Chen comments: In the Classics and their commentaries, thorough comprehension is what is valued; those who cling to a single point are bogged down and often forced in their interpretations. Does this essay not stand free amidst the multitude of exercises, independent and unleaning!

title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
噦之鳳凰肄文教於至治之區洽禮樂於太平
之境化通夷夏道塞堪輿今日之盛豈偶然哉
此蓋由我
聖天子德邁羲皇學宗周孔英資駕一世之才神用
妙萬幾之運卓卓乎帝趨而皇步蕩蕩乎天寬
而地容以圖治必基於賢能乃宵旰皇皇惟賢
是尚而已惟能是使而已彼醲仁而蓄義耕道
而獵德可以柱石吾廟廊可以股肱吾元首則
敷延厚聘俾為吾天機之燮理也忠信重祿使
===
為吾天工之寅亮也知周而才博謀訂而識遠
可以掌吾鈞衡可以分吾綸綍則量能授任収
之以依日月之光也分職授政用之以補袞職
之闕也貴而重之於焉賴以涵養吾氣質消鎮
吾邪躁信而任之於焉賴以疏附而先後奔走
而禦侮籲俊不嫌於韋布
聖明不廢於芻蕘與之陶冶天下以鑪以錘與之薰
融斯民以橐以籥由是語治效則上恬下熙矣
語天下則氷清砥平矣河海晏然揚波不驚於

此盖由我

===
爲吾天工之寅亮也知周而才博謀訏而識遠

之以位日月之光也分職授政用之以補衮職

而禦侮蕃蔽不爲於幸布

融斷民以櫜以畚由是語治效則上恬下熙矣

punctuated: 噦之鳳凰，肄文教於至治之區，洽禮樂於太平之境。化通夷夏，道塞堪輿。今日之盛，豈偶然哉？此蓋由我聖天子德邁羲皇，學宗周孔；英資駕一世之才，神用妙萬幾之運。卓卓乎帝趨而皇步，蕩蕩乎天寬而地容。以圖治必基於賢能，乃宵旰皇皇，惟賢是尚而已，惟能是使而已。彼醲仁而蓄義，耕道而獵德，可以柱石吾廟廊，可以股肱吾元首，則敷延厚聘，俾為吾天機之燮理也，忠信重祿，使為吾天工之寅亮也；知周而才博，謀訂而識遠，可以掌吾鈞衡，可以分吾綸綍，則量能授任，収之以依日月之光也，分職授政，用之以補袞職之闕也。貴而重之，於焉賴以涵養吾氣質，消鎮吾邪躁；信而任之，於焉賴以疏附而先後，奔走而禦侮。籲俊不嫌於韋布，聖明不廢於芻蕘。與之陶冶天下，以鑪以錘；與之薰融斯民，以橐以籥。由是，語治效則上恬下熙矣，語天下則氷清砥平矣。河海晏然，揚波不驚於
translation_en: … [the harmonious cry] of phoenixes, practicing cultural education in the realm of supreme governance and diffusing rites and music across a world of great peace. Moral transformation reaches both non-Chinese peoples and the Chinese heartland, and the Way fills heaven and earth. How could the flourishing of the present day be mere coincidence? This is because our sacred Son of Heaven surpasses Fuxi in virtue and takes the Duke of Zhou and Confucius as his models in learning; his heroic endowment outstrips the talents of a whole generation, and his marvelous application subtly directs the operation of the myriad affairs of state. How eminent is his imperial stride and august pace! How vast is his heaven-like breadth and earth-like tolerance! Holding that plans for governance must be founded upon the worthy and the able, he works anxiously from before dawn until late at night, simply exalting the worthy and employing the able. As for those who are steeped in benevolence and store up righteousness, who plow the Way and hunt for virtue, who can serve as pillars and cornerstones of our court and as the arms and legs of our sovereign head, he extends broad invitations and generous gifts to make them the harmonizers of our heavenly workings, and accords them loyal trust and heavy emoluments to make them the reverent illuminators of our heavenly tasks. As for those whose knowledge is comprehensive and talent broad, whose counsel is well-considered and foresight far-reaching, who can hold our balance of state and share in drafting our imperial decrees, he measures their abilities to bestow appointments, gathering them in so that they may cleave to the light of the sun and moon, and he apportions offices and entrusts administration, employing them to mend whatever is lacking in the imperial duties. Honoring and esteeming them, he thereby relies on them to nourish our temperament and to quell and subdue our perverse or rash impulses; trusting and employing them, he thereby relies on them to rally the estranged, to attend before and behind, to hasten in service, and to ward off insult. In calling forth men of eminence, he does not disdain those in leather belts and coarse cloth; in his sacred enlightenment, he does not neglect the words of grass-cutters and firewood-gatherers. With them he molds and refines the empire, as with furnace and hammer; with them he warms and blends this people, as with bellows and blowpipe. Consequently, if one speaks of the efficacy of governance, above there is tranquility and below there is joyous harmony; if one speaks of the empire, it is as pure as ice and as level as a whetstone. The Yellow River and the seas are calm, and surging waves do not startle…

title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
臣寵昵君德係焉豈可不守和乎盖過於和則流而
為同不可也吾則守和而以可濟否使拾遺補過之
各中其節不及於和則乖而為異亦不可也吾則守
和而以柔濟剛使婉詞諷諫之皆適其中如是則君
德正矣先君德而後朝廷朝廷庸可不正乎是故百
官庶僚之具瞻者宰之職也吾居宰輔之職必正色
立朝進退賢否使百僚有師師之風表儀朝著黜陟
幽明使庶位有明明之美如是則朝廷正矣朝廷固
先於天下而天下容可不慮乎是故生民休戚之所
===
===
関者大臣之位也吾處大臣之位必安不忘危惟恐
四方有一民之未遂其生思患預防惟恐天下有一
物之不得其理如是則天下平矣吁由君德以及朝
廷由朝廷以及天下無不各盡所當為則人臣事君
之道豈復有加於此哉雖然不特此也緇衣有曰故
大臣不可不敬也是民之表也邇臣不可不慎也是
民之道也合而觀之為君者不可不慎擇其人為臣
者不可不各盡其職君臣兩盡其道何患國家天下
之不治哉孟子曰有官守者盡其職有言責者盡其

For if they exceed harmony, they drift into mere conformity, which is impermissible; I therefore maintain harmony and temper the unacceptable with the acceptable, ensuring that in making good omissions and remedying faults, each action hits its proper measure. If they fall short of harmony, they become perverse and contrarian, which is also impermissible; I therefore maintain harmony and temper hardness with gentleness, ensuring that tactful words and indirect remonstrances all hit the mean. When this is so, the sovereign's virtue is rectified. Putting the sovereign's virtue first and the court after, how could the court not be rectified? Therefore, the one to whom all the hundred officials and multitudinous functionaries look up is the office of the Chief Councilor. When I occupy the office of Chief Councilor, I must stand at court with a solemn countenance, advancing the worthy and dismissing the unworthy, causing the hundred officials to have the air of emulating one another; I must serve as a model for the court ranks, demoting the benighted and promoting the enlightened, causing the multitudinous positions to possess the beauty of clear discernment. When this is so, the court is rectified. Though the court indeed comes before the realm, how could the realm not be given thought? Therefore, that upon which the weal and woe of the people depend is the position of the great ministers. When I occupy the position of a great minister, in peace I must not forget danger, only fearing lest in the four quarters there be a single person who has not fulfilled his livelihood; I must ponder calamities and guard against them in advance, only fearing lest in the realm there be a single thing that has not attained its proper order. When this is so, the realm is brought to peace. Ah! From the sovereign's virtue extending to the court, and from the court extending to the realm, in nothing failing to exhaust what ought to be done—how could the way of a minister serving his sovereign have anything to add to this? Even so, it is not only this. The "Black Robes" (Ziyi) [chapter of the Record of Rites] says: "Therefore great ministers must be respected, for they are the models of the people; close ministers must be chosen with care, for they are the guides of the people." Viewing these together, he who is the sovereign must carefully select his men, and those who are ministers must each fulfill their duties. When sovereign and minister both fulfill their proper way, what worry could there be that the state and the realm would not be well governed? title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
重譯邊境肅然風塵不灑於外夷
大化播於村謠野歌之聲
皇道談於樵童牧孺之口是盖不過端拱於穆清
之上而自雷動八荒優游於宮庭之間而自風
行四表無為之治誠振古而莫逾於今矣然愚
竊惟今日所以饗致治之盛者固成於
聖天子重光累洽之功而實本於
祖宗神化積累之久乃我
聖祖天戈一揮而腥穢掃蕩
===
太宗内難削平而綱常屹立之
二聖人者固未嘗不重賢能之用而賢能之佐於其
間亦未嘗不成非常之烈此今日所以饗致治
之盛而曠古莫加也於戲
明主之紹承重華而恊德賢能之功業前輝而後映
欲形容
國朝之盛吾恐若穹壤之難測日月之難繪矣然
太陽之升不期乎葵藿之傾而葵藿自傾和氣
之至不期乎倉庚之鳴而倉庚自鳴則甄陶

The great transformation is spread through the sounds of village ballads and rustic songs, and the Imperial Way is spoken of on the lips of woodcutter boys and herd-children. This is indeed nothing other than sitting with folded hands in serene majesty above, while thunder naturally shakes the eight extremities; moving at ease within the palace courts, while the wind naturally sweeps across the four reaches. Governance through non-action truly has never surpassed the present since antiquity! Yet I humbly reflect that the reason we today enjoy the flourishing of achieved order, while certainly accomplished through the merit of the Sacred Son of Heaven in renewing brilliance and accumulating harmony, is in truth rooted in the long accumulation of the divine transformations of the Imperial Ancestors. These two Sages never failed to value the employment of the worthy and capable, and the worthy and capable who assisted during their reigns likewise never failed to achieve extraordinary feats. This is why today we enjoy the flourishing of achieved order, unsurpassed since antiquity. Alas! text:

同考試官教諭侯　批議論反覆文思波瀾新音雅詞層見疊
出如入鄧林之野前瞻後顧莫匪良材
如登崑崙之岡近取遠求無非美玉論塲
如此自當歛衽
同考試官學正朱　批筆力勁健文勢浩瀚不啻大川長江平
鋪滉流莫知底極觀者無不起望洋之嘆
且末引孔孟不得用為説讀之使人躍然真
傑作也
考試官侍讀尹　批此論超今軼古英氣逼人令人一見自當刮
目蓋塲中之空群者髙薦何忝
考試官學士陳　批論作四書義者多矣求其脫迹凡近接軫古
作如此篇者可多見乎
天生賢才豈偶然哉將以為世之人主共理以
致治也然其生也固本於天而其出而為世用
punctuated:
聖化者，豈能自已於言哉！愚請假高岡鳴鳳之歌，以誦於鳶飛魚躍之下。

又
同考試官教諭侯批：議論反覆，文思波瀾，新音雅詞，層見疊出。如入鄧林之野，前瞻後顧，莫匪良材；如登崑崙之岡，近取遠求，無非美玉。論塲如此，自當斂衽。
同考試官學正朱批：筆力勁健，文勢浩瀚，不啻大川長江，平鋪漫流，莫知底極，觀者無不起望洋之嘆。且末引孔孟不得用為說，讀之使人躍然，真傑作也。
考試官侍讀尹批：此論超今軼古，英氣逼人，令人一見自當刮目，盖塲中之空群者，高薦何忝！
考試官學士陳批：論作四書義者多矣，求其脫迹凡近、接軫古作如此篇者，可多見乎？

天生賢才，豈偶然哉！將以為世之人主共理以致治也。然其生也固本於天，而其出而為世用
translation_en:
… the sage's transformative influence—how could they keep themselves from speaking out? I beg to borrow the song of the phoenix singing on the high ridge, to chant beneath where the kites fly and the fishes leap.

title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
也則不在於天焉故必有非常之主而後有非
常之人有非常之人而後有非常之治也苟世
之人主不能順乎天而使賢才之𠇗生則無以
為致治之本矣其欲享夫非常之治也豈不甚
難矣乎愚嘗伏讀
宣宗章皇帝御製五倫書所載荀况之言而有以知
其㫖矣請申論之世之論治者孰不曰號令嚴
明法度修舉可以致治矣若此者以為飾治之
末則可而致治之本則不在於此焉孰不曰勞
===
心焦思宵衣旰食足以致治矣若此者以為致
治之本固可而其致治之盛則不全以此焉使
徒以法為足以致治則秦政之苛刻非無法也
何天下二世而已使徒以勤為足以致治則隋
文之傳餐非不勤也何天下再傳而已夫天下
之治既不在法又不在勤為人君者將欲饗其
至盛之治也抑何從而得乎其必有本也盍亦
觀夫技藝者焉夫規矩者成方圓之器也不以
規矩則雖巧如公輸而無以成方圓矣六律者

也，則不在於天焉。故必有非常之主，而後有非常之人；有非常之人，而後有非常之治也。苟世之人主不能順乎天而使賢才之𠇗生，則無以為致治之本矣；其欲享夫非常之治也，豈不甚難矣乎？愚嘗伏讀宣宗章皇帝御製《五倫書》所載荀况之言，而有以知其㫖矣，請申論之。
世之論治者，孰不曰號令嚴明、法度修舉，可以致治矣？若此者，以為飾治之末則可，而致治之本則不在於此焉。孰不曰勞心焦思、宵衣旰食，足以致治矣？若此者，以為致治之本固可，而其致治之盛則不全以此焉。使徒以法為足以致治，則秦政之苛刻，非無法也，何天下二世而已？使徒以勤為足以致治，則隋文之傳餐，非不勤也，何天下再傳而已？夫天下之治，既不在法，又不在勤，為人君者，將欲饗其至盛之治也，抑何從而得乎？其必有本也。盍亦觀夫技藝者焉？夫規矩者，成方圓之器也；不以規矩，則雖巧如公輸，而無以成方圓矣。六律者，
translation_en:
… does not depend on Heaven. Therefore, only when there is an extraordinary ruler can there be extraordinary men; and only when there are extraordinary men can there be extraordinary governance. If the rulers of the world cannot comply with Heaven and thus cause worthy talents to be born in vain, they will lack the fundamental basis for bringing about good governance; should they then wish to enjoy extraordinary governance, would that not be exceedingly difficult? I have humbly read the words of Xun Kuang 荀況 recorded in the Book of the Five Human Relationships (Wulun shu 五倫書), imperially composed by Emperor Zhang of the Xuanzong 宣宗 temple name [the Xuande Emperor], and have thereby come to understand their purport; allow me to elaborate on this in a discourse.

Among those in the world who discuss governance, who does not say that when commands are strict and clear and laws and institutions are well-maintained, good governance can be achieved? Such things may be regarded as the superficial adornments of governance, yet the root of achieving good governance does not lie therein. Who does not say that laboring one's mind and fretting in thought, dressing before dawn and eating after dusk, are sufficient to achieve good governance? Such things may indeed be regarded as a basis for achieving governance, yet the flourishing perfection of governance does not rest wholly upon this. If one merely took laws to be sufficient to bring about good governance, then the harshness of Zheng of Qin 秦政 [the First Emperor of Qin] was certainly not lacking in laws—why did his realm last for only two generations? If one merely took diligence to be sufficient to bring about good governance, then Emperor Wen of Sui 隋文 having his meals passed to him while working was certainly not lacking in diligence—why was his realm passed down only once? Now, since the governance of the empire lies neither in laws nor in diligence, if a ruler of men wishes to enjoy the most flourishing governance, from where, then, is he to obtain it? It must have a root. Why not also observe those who practice skilled crafts? Now, the compass and square are the instruments for making circles and squares; without using the compass and square, even someone as skillful as Gongshu 公輸 [Gongshu Ban] would have no means to form squares and circles. The six pitch-pipes are…

title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
正五音之器也不以六律則雖聰如師曠無以
正五音矣技藝且爾况天下乎盖賢才者治天
下之利器也不以賢才則雖聖如堯舜而無補
於治焉故明君之治乎民也聰明而睿知體天
以行道其意以為賢而有德者足以尊主而庇
民乃天之所以與我共理天下者也使我而不
尚之則褻乎天矣能而有才者足以脩政而立
事亦天之所以與我共理庶事者也使我而不
使之則逆乎天矣褻天不可也逆天亦不可也
===
於是賢而有德者則尊而尚之尚不徒尚而必
與之共天位焉能而有才者則任而使之使不
徒使而必與之治天職焉建官惟賢位事惟能
不才者不得以倖進賢者在位能者在職不肖
者不得以苟禄夫賢者尚之則賢者樂於進用
而咸有帝臣之願能者使之則能者勤於吏事
而咸有効力之心内而朝廷之上有都俞吁咈
之風外而州郡之間有慈祥豈弟之政措國家
於泰山之安躋斯民於仁壽之域君之黎民無

punctuated: 正五音之器也，不以六律，則雖聰如師曠，無以正五音矣。技藝且爾，况天下乎？盖賢才者，治天下之利器也；不以賢才，則雖聖如堯、舜，而無補於治焉。故明君之治乎民也，聰明而睿知，體天以行道。其意以為賢而有德者，足以尊主而庇民，乃天之所以與我共理天下者也，使我而不尚之，則褻乎天矣；能而有才者，足以脩政而立事，亦天之所以與我共理庶事者也，使我而不使之，則逆乎天矣。褻天不可也，逆天亦不可也。於是賢而有德者，則尊而尚之，尚不徒尚，而必與之共天位焉；能而有才者，則任而使之，使不徒使，而必與之治天職焉。建官惟賢，位事惟能，不才者不得以倖進；賢者在位，能者在職，不肖者不得以苟禄。夫賢者尚之，則賢者樂於進用，而咸有帝臣之願；能者使之，則能者勤於吏事，而咸有効力之心。内而朝廷之上，有都俞吁咈之風；外而州郡之間，有慈祥豈弟之政。措國家於泰山之安，躋斯民於仁壽之域。君之黎民無
translation_en:
… are the instruments for rectifying the five musical tones; without using the six pitch-pipes, even someone with hearing as acute as Shi Kuang 師曠 would have no means to rectify the five tones. If even technical arts are like this, how much more so the realm! For worthy and talented men are the sharp instruments for governing the realm; without using worthy and talented men, even someone as sage as Yao 堯 or Shun 舜 would be of no help to governance. Therefore, when an enlightened ruler governs the people, he is perceptive, clear-sighted, and wise, embodying Heaven in practicing the Way. In his mind, he considers that those who are worthy and possess virtue are sufficient to honor the sovereign and shelter the people; they are the ones Heaven has given to govern the realm together with him. "Should I fail to esteem them, that would be to profane Heaven." And those who are capable and possess talent are sufficient to cultivate administration and establish enterprises; they too are the ones Heaven has given to manage the myriad affairs together with him. "Should I fail to employ them, that would be to defy Heaven." To profane Heaven is impermissible, and to defy Heaven is likewise impermissible.

Thereupon, as for those who are worthy and possess virtue, he honors and esteems them—and in esteeming them, he does not merely esteem them in name, but 반드시 shares with them the Heaven-ordained positions. As for those who are capable and possess talent, he trusts and employs them—and in employing them, he does not merely employ them casually, but necessarily charges them with governing the Heaven-ordained offices. In establishing offices, he seeks only the worthy; in assigning affairs, he seeks only the capable, so that the untalented cannot advance through luck. With the worthy in high positions and the capable in office, the unworthy cannot illicitly draw emoluments. Now, when the worthy are esteemed, the worthy rejoice in being advanced and employed, and all cherish the aspiration to be ministers to a sage emperor; when the capable are employed, the capable are diligent in administrative affairs, and all harbor the desire to exert their strength. Within, at court above, there is the ethos of harmonious affirmation and frank remonstrance; without, among the prefectures and commanderies, there is benevolent, kind, and genial administration. This places the state upon the security of Mount Tai and raises the people to the realm of benevolence and longevity. Of the ruler's black-haired people, none…

title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
不安君之子孫無不保由是人君之居上端冕
凝旒不待有所作為也而海宇自成雍煕之治
垂衣拱手不待有所經營也而天下自成咸和
之俗不必嚴刑峻法而求一梗化敗俗者無有
焉不必宵衣旰食而求一妨政害治者無有焉
但見皇風宣布於六合而乾清坤寧萬物勃勃
然也但見王化漸被於四表而鳶飛魚躍品彙
煕煕然也仰之為父母戴之為元后不以遠近
而殊不以華夏而異所謂凡有血氣莫不尊親
===
者此也萬壽無疆福祿攸宜不啻如日升而月
恒不啻如山峙而川增所謂自天祐之吉無不
利者此也明主饗其盛也何如哉向使褻天而
不尚賢逆天而不使能是猶為方圓而不以規
矩正五音而不以六律也其欲天下治且不可
況望於饗其盛乎故人君不患不饗其盛而患
天下之未治不患天下之不治而患賢才之未
用為人君者不欲饗其盛則已欲饗其盛而不
尚賢使能何以哉若賢才者其治天下之本乎

translation_en: … is not at peace, and none of the ruler's descendants is not protected. Therefore, the ruler, occupying his supreme position, wears his ceremonial cap upright with its jade pendants hanging still, and without needing to take deliberate action, the realm within the seas naturally achieves an order of harmonious prosperity; letting his robes hang down and folding his hands, without needing to busy himself with planning, the world naturally forms customs of universal concord. There is no need for severe punishments and harsh laws, yet if one looks for a single person who obstructs moral transformation or corrupts customs, none is to be found; there is no need to dress before dawn and eat after dusk, yet if one looks for a single person who impedes administration or harms governance, none is to be found. One sees only the august influence spreading throughout the six directions, Heaven clear and Earth tranquil, and the myriad things flourishing vigorously; one sees only the kingly transformation gradually reaching to the four borders, kites flying and fishes leaping, and all categories of beings thriving joyfully. People look up to him as father and mother and revere him as their great sovereign, without distinction between near and far, and without difference between Chinese and non-Chinese [?]; this is what is meant by "All who have blood and breath cannot but honor and love him." Enjoying boundless longevity and fitting blessings and emoluments, it is not merely like the rising of the sun and the waxing of the moon, nor merely like the towering of mountains and the swelling of rivers; this is what is meant by "Help comes to him from Heaven; there will be good fortune, and nothing that is not beneficial." How magnificent is the enlightened ruler's enjoyment of such flourishing! Suppose instead that he were to slight Heaven and fail to esteem the worthy, or defy Heaven and fail to employ the capable—this would be like trying to make squares and circles without compass and square, or rectifying the five notes without the six pitch-pipes. Even if he wished the world to be well governed, it would be impossible; how much less could he hope to enjoy its flourishing? Therefore, a ruler does not worry about failing to enjoy its flourishing, but worries that the world is not yet well governed; he does not worry that the world is not well governed, but worries that worthy talents are not yet employed. For one who is a ruler, if he does not wish to enjoy its flourishing, then let the matter rest; if he wishes to enjoy its flourishing and yet does not esteem the worthy and employ the capable, how can he do so? As for worthy talents, are they not the root of governing the world…

text:
其為明主之所以饗其盛者乎或曰賢才之生
不世出也幸有唐虞三代之人才則為之君者
足以享唐虞三代之盛矣其不幸而僅止於漢
唐宋之人才則其治止於漢唐宋而已欲享其
盛得乎噫不然也賢才之生何代無之但其生
也不偶生故其出也不輕出使世無人君尚而
使之則寧考槃澗阿棲遲巖谷必不為之用而
成其盛治矣故非堯舜禹湯文武之君則亦何
以尚賢使能而享唐虞三代之盛乎不然春秋
===
之時非不有孔子也而春秋之君不能饗其盛
戰國之時非不有孟子也而戰國之君亦不能
饗其盛所以然者其於尚賢使能之說漠乎其
無聞也方今天下蠻夷率服四海一家
聖天子在上端拱無為以饗至盛之治實以
體天行道尚賢使能之所致也豈特唐虞三代
之君專美於前哉愚也何幸躬逢其盛
又 陳瓊

punctuated:
其為明主之所以饗其盛者乎！或曰：「賢才之生，不世出也。幸有唐、虞、三代之人才，則為之君者足以享唐、虞、三代之盛矣；其不幸而僅止於漢、唐、宋之人才，則其治止於漢、唐、宋而已，欲享其盛，得乎？」噫！不然也。賢才之生，何代無之？但其生也不偶生，故其出也不輕出。使世無人君尚而使之，則寧考槃澗阿、棲遲巖谷，必不為之用而成其盛治矣。故非堯、舜、禹、湯、文、武之君，則亦何以尚賢使能而享唐、虞、三代之盛乎？不然，春秋之時非不有孔子也，而春秋之君不能饗其盛；戰國之時非不有孟子也，而戰國之君亦不能饗其盛。所以然者，其於尚賢使能之說，漠乎其無聞也。方今天下，蠻夷率服，四海一家，聖天子在上，端拱無為，以饗至盛之治，實以體天行道、尚賢使能之所致也，豈特唐、虞、三代之君專美於前哉！愚也何幸，躬逢其盛！
又 陳瓊
translation_en:
…Are they not that whereby an enlightened ruler enjoys such flourishing? Someone may say: "Men of worth and talent are not born in every generation. If one is fortunate enough to have the men of talent of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties, then the ruler suffices to enjoy the flourishing of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties; if one is unfortunate and has only the men of talent of the Han, Tang, and Song, then one's governance stops at that of the Han, Tang, and Song—should one wish to enjoy that supreme flourishing, could it be attained?" Alas, it is not so! What dynasty lacks the birth of men of worth and talent? Yet because they are not born by mere chance, they do not come forth lightly. Were there no ruler in the world to esteem and employ them, they would rather build their huts in mountain gullies and linger in rocky valleys; they would certainly refuse to be used by him to bring about his flourishing governance. Therefore, without rulers like Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu, how could one esteem the worthy and employ the capable so as to enjoy the flourishing of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties? Otherwise, the Spring and Autumn period was not without Confucius, yet the rulers of the Spring and Autumn period could not enjoy such flourishing; the Warring States period was not without Mencius, yet the rulers of the Warring States could not enjoy such flourishing either. The reason for this is that, regarding the doctrine of esteeming the worthy and employing the capable, they remained utterly indifferent and deaf to it. Today throughout the world, the barbarian tribes all submit, and all within the Four Seas are one family. The Sacred Son of Heaven reigns above, sitting with folded hands in non-action to enjoy the most flourishing governance; this is truly brought about by embodying Heaven, practicing the Way, esteeming the worthy, and employing the capable. How could the rulers of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties alone monopolize such glory in the past! How fortunate am I, in my humble simplicity, to witness this flourishing in person!

Another [discourse], by Chen Qiong 陳瓊

title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
同考試官訓導葉批此篇僅千餘字文勢變化畧無定蹤而孚澤
於理譬之春氣方至千葩萬卉殊形異狀皆造
化中物且讀之無一字艱滯自不覺其詞之繁
也論場如此豈易得哉
同考試官教諭王批一論自肺腑中沛然流出殊不見斧鑿痕讀之
剰有旨味可雋永也取之以為專事造語者戒
考試官侍讀尹批南畿人材淵藪摛詞立論鮮有弗能求其脫去
場屋陳腐之氣駸駸尋古作如此篇者指未許
多屈也可以得之晚而不錄乎
===
考試官學士陳批既得前論已為奇矣此篇復出尤覺有味商
敦夏彝不能舎此取彼故并錄之
論曰穀與粟飢者皆欲食而致之者必先事乎
耒耜布與帛寒者皆欲衣而致之者必先事乎
機杼至治馨香君人者皆欲饗之也然不先乎
尚賢使能又何以致之哉何也工欲善其事必
先利其器賢能者國家之利器穀粟之耒耜布
帛之機杼也穀粟而非耒耜一腹之飢且不能
充而欲儲侍之盈可乎布帛而非機杼一身之

punctuated:
同考試官訓導葉批：此篇僅千餘字，文勢變化，畧無定蹤，而孚澤於理。譬之春氣方至，千葩萬卉，殊形異狀，皆造化中物。且讀之無一字艱滯，自不覺其詞之繁也。論場如此，豈易得哉！
同考試官教諭王批：一論自肺腑中沛然流出，殊不見斧鑿痕，讀之剰有旨味可雋永也。取之以為專事造語者戒。
考試官侍讀尹批：南畿人材淵藪，摛詞立論，鮮有弗能。求其脫去場屋陳腐之氣，駸駸尋古作如此篇者，指未許多屈也。可以得之晚而不錄乎？
考試官學士陳批：既得前論，已為奇矣；此篇復出，尤覺有味。商敦夏彝，不能舎此取彼，故并錄之。
論曰：穀與粟，飢者皆欲食，而致之者必先事乎耒耜；布與帛，寒者皆欲衣，而致之者必先事乎機杼；至治馨香，君人者皆欲饗之也，然不先乎尚賢使能，又何以致之哉？何也？「工欲善其事，必先利其器。」賢能者，國家之利器，穀粟之耒耜，布帛之機杼也。穀粟而非耒耜，一腹之飢且不能充，而欲儲侍之盈，可乎？布帛而非機杼，一身之
translation_en:
Comment by Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor Ye: This piece is only a little over a thousand characters long; the momentum of its prose shifts and transforms without any fixed track, yet it is thoroughly imbued with principle. It is like when the breath of spring first arrives: a thousand blossoms and ten thousand plants, of diverse forms and varied shapes, are all things produced within nature's creative transformation. Moreover, in reading it, there is not a single character that is labored or sluggish, so one naturally does not feel that its words are prolix. In the examination hall for discourses, how could something like this be easily obtained!
Comment by Associate Examiner and Instructor Wang: The entire discourse flows forth copiously from the depths of the heart, showing no trace of the chisel or axe; reading it leaves an abundant, lingering flavor of deep meaning to be savored. We select it to serve as a warning to those who devote themselves solely to artificial phrasing.
Comment by Examiner and Reader-in-waiting Yin: The Southern Metropolitan Region is a deep reservoir of talent; in spreading forth phrases and establishing discourses, few are incapable. Yet if one seeks those who have shed the stale and hackneyed air of the examination halls and press briskly toward the works of antiquity like this piece, one cannot bend many fingers in counting them. How could we fail to record it just because we came upon it late?
Comment by Examiner and Academician Chen: Having already obtained the preceding discourse, we considered it extraordinary; when this piece also appeared, it felt even more flavorful. Like the *dui* vessels of the Shang and the *yi* vessels of the Xia, we could not abandon one to take the other, and therefore we have recorded both of them together.
The discourse reads: Grain and millet—all who are hungry wish to eat them, yet to bring them about one must first attend to the plowshare and plow-handle. Hemp cloth and silk—all who are cold wish to wear them, yet to bring them about one must first attend to the loom and shuttle. The fragrant aroma of supreme governance—all who rule over men wish to enjoy it, yet if they do not first exalt the worthy and employ the capable, how can they bring it about? Why is this? "When a craftsman wishes to do his work well, he must first sharpen his tools." The worthy and the capable are the sharp tools of the state, the plowshare and plow-handle of grain and millet, the loom and shuttle of hemp cloth and silk. If one seeks grain and millet without plowshare and plow-handle, one cannot even fill a single hungry belly—could one then wish for the granaries and stores to be full? If one seeks hemp cloth and silk without loom and shuttle, even the… of a single body…

title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
寒且不能禦而欲帑藏之溢得乎君而舍賢才
以治亦猶是耳此明主所以尚賢使能而後克
饗其盛歟荀子之言厥有旨矣請發其旨而論
之天下如此其大也兆民如此其眾也庶政如
此其繁也人君一身如此其眇也欲嚮其治茲
亦難矣禮樂刑政闕一職則天工廢矣未可以
饗其盛工虞教養無其人則天職弛矣未可以
饗其盛智巧相攻勇力相抗失其治未可以言
饗富者吞貧辯者惑眾失其治未可以言饗善
===
治者則有致饗之道徳之盛者則折節以下之
而不肖者弗禮人之能者則分職以布之而不
才者不任禮樂刑政工虞教養充之者惟賢才
也籠智巧挫勇力鋤富強闢邪說范之者惟賢
才也吾見其刑政禮樂燦然而脩明工虞教養
秩然而振舉曰脩明曰振舉皆賢才之所致也
吾見其智如良平失其智勇如賁育失其勇富
如晉楚不能施辯如儀秦不能逞勇與智皆失
富與辯莫逞皆賢才之所致也豈惟得此隨事

饗其盛歟荀子之言厥有旨矣請發其旨而論

punctuated: 寒且不能禦，而欲帑藏之溢，得乎？君而舍賢才以治，亦猶是耳。此明主所以尚賢使能，而後克饗其盛歟！《荀子》之言，厥有旨矣，請發其旨而論之。天下如此其大也，兆民如此其眾也，庶政如此其繁也，人君一身如此其眇也，欲嚮其治，茲亦難矣。禮樂刑政，闕一職則天工廢矣，未可以饗其盛；工虞教養，無其人則天職弛矣，未可以饗其盛。智巧相攻，勇力相抗，失其治，未可以言饗；富者吞貧，辯者惑眾，失其治，未可以言饗。善治者則有致饗之道。徳之盛者，則折節以下之，而不肖者弗禮；人之能者，則分職以布之，而不才者不任。禮樂刑政、工虞教養，充之者惟賢才也；籠智巧、挫勇力、鋤富強、闢邪說，范之者惟賢才也。吾見其刑政禮樂燦然而脩明，工虞教養秩然而振舉；曰脩明、曰振舉，皆賢才之所致也。吾見其智如良、平失其智，勇如賁、育失其勇，富如晉、楚不能施，辯如儀、秦不能逞；勇與智皆失，富與辯莫逞，皆賢才之所致也。豈惟得此隨事
translation_en:
…even ward off the cold of a single body, yet to wish for the treasuries to overflow—how could that be attained? For a ruler to cast aside worthy talents in seeking to govern is just like this. Is this not why an enlightened ruler esteems the worthy and employs the capable, and only afterward is able to enjoy the fullness of order? The words of Xunzi indeed have deep meaning; allow me to bring forth their meaning and discuss it.

The realm under heaven is so vast, the millions of people are so multitude, the myriad affairs of governance are so intricate, and the ruler's own person is so solitary; to wish to turn toward and enjoy its good order is difficult indeed. In rites, music, punishments, and administration, if a single office is lacking, then Heaven's work is neglected, and one cannot yet enjoy its fullness; in public works, forestry and wildlife management, education, and nourishment, if there are no suitable men, then Heaven's duties become lax, and one cannot yet enjoy its fullness. When the clever and cunning attack one another, and the brave and strong resist one another, good order is lost, and one cannot speak of enjoying it; when the rich swallow up the poor, and the sophists delude the multitude, good order is lost, and one cannot speak of enjoying it.

He who is skilled at governing possesses the Way to bring about that enjoyment. Toward those of abundant virtue, he bends his own standing and humbles himself before them, while the unworthy he does not treat with courtesy; as for men of capability, he apportions offices and distributes them throughout, while the untalented he does not employ. Rites, music, punishments, administration, public works, forestry, education, and nourishment—those who fill these roles are none other than worthy talents; corralling the clever and cunning, blunting the brave and strong, weeding out the rich and powerful, and refuting perverse doctrines—those who mold and restrain them are none other than worthy talents.

I see punishments, administration, rites, and music brilliantly cultivated and clarified, and public works, forestry, education, and nourishment orderly roused and promoted; this cultivation and clarification, this rousing and promotion, are all brought about by worthy talents. I see those as wise as Zhang Liang 張良 and Chen Ping 陳平 lose their cunning, those as brave as Meng Ben 孟賁 and Xia Yu 夏育 lose their valor, those as wealthy as Jin 晉 and Chu 楚 unable to deploy their wealth, and those as eloquent as Zhang Yi 張儀 and Su Qin 蘇秦 unable to indulge their sophistry; that bravery and cunning both fail, and wealth and eloquence cannot prevail, is all brought about by worthy talents. How could a ruler merely obtain such worthy talents who…

title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
致功之賢才而安於小成耶明君推是心而上
之尊德樂道以為不如是不足以有為由是將
必有大臣者出焉是以震撼擊撞而鎮定者有
其人辛甘燥濕而調齊者有其人盤錯棼結而
解紓者有其人黯闇汚濁而茹納者有其人得
是人而處之朝廷之上譽望足以服人之邪心
容色足以消人之逸志如泰山喬嶽雖無運動
之勞不疾而速不行而至靡然從風矣明君於
此其責始盡其欲始遂但垂衣拱手而已耳端
===
冕凝旒而已耳天地自位萬物自育四靈畢至
而卷阿之鳳凰不得專美於周鳥獸之蹌蹌不
獨見頌於虞易曰見龍在田天下文明詩曰無
競維人四方其訓之可誣乎哉孟子有見於此
而曰君用之則安富尊榮周子有見於此而曰
賢才輔則天下治理固然矣吾嘗悲夫人君負
於賢才而賢才負於人君者皆不能無譏也觀
夫秦始用斯高秦何負於斯高而斯高誘以刑
名濟之暴虐卒使六國亡秦孔孟仕於齊魯孔

punctuated: 致功之賢才，而安於小成耶？明君推是心而上之，尊德樂道，以為不如是不足以有為。由是將必有大臣者出焉。是以震撼擊撞而鎮定者有其人，辛甘燥濕而調齊者有其人，盤錯棼結而解紓者有其人，黯闇汚濁而茹納者有其人。得是人而處之朝廷之上，譽望足以服人之邪心，容色足以消人之逸志，如泰山喬嶽，雖無運動之勞，不疾而速，不行而至，靡然從風矣。明君於此，其責始盡，其欲始遂，但垂衣拱手而已耳，端冕凝旒而已耳。天地自位，萬物自育，四靈畢至，而《卷阿》之鳳凰不得專美於周，鳥獸之蹌蹌不獨見頌於虞。《易》曰：「見龍在田，天下文明。」《詩》曰：「無競維人，四方其訓之。」可誣乎哉？孟子有見於此，而曰：「君用之，則安富尊榮。」周子有見於此，而曰：「賢才輔，則天下治。」理固然矣。吾嘗悲夫人君負於賢才，而賢才負於人君者，皆不能無譏也。觀夫秦始用斯、高，秦何負於斯、高？而斯、高誘以刑名，濟之暴虐，卒使六國亡秦。孔、孟仕於齊、魯，孔、
translation_en: … worthy talents who achieve merit in individual matters, and rest content with minor accomplishments? The enlightened ruler extends this mind further upward, honoring virtue and delighting in the Way, believing that without doing so, it is insufficient to accomplish great things. From this, there will surely emerge great ministers. Thus, when there is shaking, battering, and collision, there are those who bring calm and stability; when there is pungency, sweetness, dryness, and dampness, there are those who harmonize and balance them; when things are gnarled, twisted, tangled, and knotted, there are those who untangle and relieve them; when there is darkness, obscurity, filth, and turbidity, there are those who tolerate and encompass them. Having obtained such men and placed them at court, their reputation and prestige suffice to subdue people's wicked hearts, and their countenance and demeanor suffice to dispel people's wayward ambitions. Like Mount Tai and the lofty peaks, though they exert no labor of movement, they are swift without hurrying, arrive without walking, and all bend before their wind. Only at this point is the enlightened ruler's responsibility fulfilled and his desire realized; he merely lets his robes hang down and folds his hands, wearing his ceremonial cap straight with its jade pendants still—nothing more. Heaven and earth naturally abide in their positions, the myriad things are naturally nourished, and the four numinous creatures all arrive; thus the phoenixes of the "Juan'e" ode cannot monopolize glory for the Zhou, and the dancing of birds and beasts is not praised solely in the time of Yu. The Classic of Changes (Yi) says: "The dragon appears in the field; all under heaven is civilized and bright." The Classic of Odes (Shi) says: "What is most powerful is being a true man; the four quarters take him as their model." Can this be false? Mencius (Mengzi) saw this truth and said: "If a ruler employs them, he will gain peace, wealth, honor, and glory." Master Zhou (Zhou Dunyi) saw this truth and said: "When worthy talents assist, all under heaven is well governed." The principle is inherently so. I have often lamented that when a ruler fails worthy talents, or when worthy talents fail their ruler, neither can escape criticism. Consider how the First Emperor of Qin employed Li Si and Zhao Gao: how did Qin fail Si and Gao? Yet Si and Gao enticed him with harsh laws and penalties and abetted his tyranny, ultimately causing the six states to destroy Qin. Confucius and Mencius served in Qi and Lu; Confucius…

title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
孟無負於齊魯而齊魯不克終用卒使終身不
遇人君負於賢才而欲饗其盛則猶烏之白馬
之角固不可得賢才負於人君而欲饗其盛則
猶蜀之日越之雪亦可得乎故曰上下交而德
業成如此此明主之欲饗其盛必自賢才始猶
飢者之穀粟寒者之布帛必于耒耜必于機杼
也論而至是則知治其事者必先得其本得其
本必先善其具古之饗盛治者莫堯舜若也觀
其比屋可封而黎民有於變之風四方風動而
===
萬國有咸寧之美迹其所由則在朝者皆三德
六德之賢曰俊曰乂之士向非賢才輔可以一
而獨治乎古之饗盛治者亦莫禹湯若也觀其
山川鬼神亦莫不寧鳥獸魚鼈咸若受天明命
以有九有之師迹其所自則在職者皆惟賢惟
能之士克宅克俊之賢向非賢才輔可以一人
而獨理乎噫堯舜禹湯善其具者然也下而漢
唐宋莫不由此以饗其治夫何疑乎方今
聖人在上萬方率服四夷咸賓雍熈太和之盛曠漢

punctuated: 孟無負於齊魯，而齊魯不克終用，卒使終身不遇。人君負於賢才而欲饗其盛，則猶烏之白、馬之角，固不可得；賢才負於人君而欲饗其盛，則猶蜀之日、越之雪，亦可得乎？故曰：「上下交而德業成。」如此，此明主之欲饗其盛，必自賢才始，猶飢者之穀粟、寒者之布帛，必于耒耜、必于機杼也。論而至是，則知治其事者必先得其本，得其本必先善其具。古之饗盛治者，莫堯、舜若也。觀其比屋可封，而黎民有於變之風；四方風動，而萬國有咸寧之美。迹其所由，則在朝者皆三德、六德之賢，曰俊、曰乂之士。向非賢才輔，可以一而獨治乎？古之饗盛治者，亦莫禹、湯若也。觀其山川鬼神亦莫不寧，鳥獸魚鼈咸若，受天明命，以有九有之師。迹其所自，則在職者皆惟賢惟能之士，克宅克俊之賢。向非賢才輔，可以一人而獨理乎？噫！堯、舜、禹、湯善其具者然也，下而漢、唐、宋莫不由此以饗其治，夫何疑乎？方今聖人在上，萬方率服，四夷咸賓，雍熈太和之盛，曠漢、
translation_en:
…and Mencius did not fail Qi and Lu, yet Qi and Lu could not employ them to the end, ultimately causing them to go through their whole lives without meeting a worthy ruler. When a ruler fails worthy talents and yet wishes to enjoy flourishing rule, it is like the whiteness of a crow or the horns of a horse—something certainly impossible to obtain. When worthy talents fail their ruler and he yet wishes to enjoy flourishing rule, it is like the sun in Shu or the snow in Yue—how could that be obtained either? Therefore it is said: "When above and below are in communion, virtue and great enterprise are accomplished." Being thus, an enlightened ruler who wishes to enjoy flourishing rule must begin with worthy talents, just as grain for the hungry and cloth and silk for the cold must come from the plowshare and the loom.

Reasoning to this point, one knows that he who would govern affairs must first grasp the root, and to grasp the root he must first perfect his instruments. Among those in antiquity who enjoyed flourishing rule, none equaled Yao and Shun. Observe how every household was worthy of enfeoffment, and the black-haired people had the custom of transforming toward goodness; the four quarters were moved as by the wind, and the myriad states possessed the beauty of universal peace. Tracing whence this came, those at court were all worthies of the Three Virtues and Six Virtues, gentlemen called men of eminence and men of ability. Had they not been assisted by worthy talents, could they have governed alone by themselves? Among those in antiquity who enjoyed flourishing rule, none equaled Yu and Tang either. Observe how even the mountains, rivers, ghosts, and spirits were none of them unpeaceful, while birds, beasts, fishes, and turtles all conformed to their natures; and how they received the bright mandate of Heaven to possess the multitudes of the Nine Regions. Tracing whence this arose, those in office were all gentlemen solely of worth and ability, worthies able to occupy their posts and show eminent virtue. Had they not been assisted by worthy talents, could a single man have brought order alone? Ah! Such was the way Yao, Shun, Yu, and Tang perfected their instruments. Coming down to the Han, Tang, and Song, none did not follow this path to enjoy good governance—what doubt can there be?

At present, a Sage is on high; the myriad regions submit and obey, and the four barbarous tribes all come as guests. The flourishing of harmonious brightness and great peace is unprecedented in the Han,…

朕稽唐、虞之治，必以得人為盛。故元愷舉而庶績熙，黎獻臣而九功叙。朕以菲德，受天明命，夙夜祗懼，思得吉士，以與共理。咨爾在位，蓋已有年，而賢才未盡登用。豈貢舉之條未至歟？抑奉行之人弗虔歟？茲特申命，爾其清乃心，恪乃事。職郡國者，務求遺逸；司貢舉者，毋事虛文。如或安常習故，邦有常刑。欽哉毋替！

We have examined the governance of Tang [Yao] and Yu [Shun], and found that its flourishing always lay in obtaining the right men. Thus, when the "Eight Worthies" (Yuankai) were promoted, all achievements were resplendent; when the eminent men among the multitude submitted as subjects, the Nine Services were brought into order. With Our meager virtue, We have received the bright Mandate of Heaven. Morning and night We stand in reverent awe, longing to obtain admirable gentlemen with whom to share in governance. Oh, you who hold office! It has now been some years, yet worthy talents have not all been advanced and employed. Is it that the regulations for recommendation and presentation are not yet thorough? Or is it that those who carry them out lack devotion? Now We specially reiterate Our command: purify your hearts and be reverent in your duties. Those who administer the commanderies and principalities must strive to seek out the overlooked and retired; those who are in charge of recommendations and presentations must not indulge in empty formalities. Should anyone remain complacent in routine and bound by old habits, the state has its regular punishments. Respect this, and do not be remiss!

Memorial (Biao)

Your servant [Qian] Ruoshui states: On a certain day of this month, a certain official named so-and-so respectfully proclaimed the Imperial decree appointing your servant so-and-so as a Hanlin Academician. Your servant, truly fearful and truly trembling, bows his head to the ground again and again, and humbly submits this statement: The Golden Flower Department and the White Jade Hall have long attached great weight to the selection of the "Northern Gate" scholars; the Purple Forbidden Enclosure and the Rue-Fragrant Pavilion revere the solemnity of the Eastern Lodge. Lofty and ethereal, they rest close beside the Bowl of the Northern Dipper; deep and secluded, they frequently hear the Imperial words. Were one not an eminent scholar, one would sully this pure rank. The Great Potter has grandly bestowed His molding and refining, yet a small vessel truly finds it difficult to bear the load. Examining my heart, I know shame; patting myself, I feel as though startled. This all comes from humbly encountering [His Majesty the Emperor], of divine martiality and sagely civility, of deep counsel and heroic decisiveness. With open sincerity You accept remonstrance, following the ancient ethos of loving to question and loving to examine; economizing on expenditures and cherishing the people, You truly accord with the Way of being able to be frugal and diligent. Having pacified all within the seas, Your achievements and enterprises shine forth in upholding human relations [?]; holding former Confucian scholars in high esteem, …

哉鉛槧之薄習循行數墨猥矣章句之陋儒方
自憐襪線之短才何以塞
===
絲綸之重任
玉音面諭謂清要貴重朕不得為
爾衮曰官謂拖紫紆朱族皆延賞既遭時而得位
當報國以竭誠以〔臣〕之愚於心猶歉竊惟高尚
之士固不以名位為寵榮忠正之流亦不以窮
達易志操寔惟素蘊況值
清時必資寵遇於身方欲效忠於
上是特中人以下之事固非忠正高尚之為〔臣〕當日
就月將非堯舜之道不敢陳
punctuated: 道德巍乎其莫及。首專相業，衆正足以勝愉邪；日御經筵，一性不移於近習。人皆滿望，史不絶書。誠太平有道之君，真端拱無為之聖。是以海隅日出之地，悉仰帝徳之光；於凡際天所覆之邦，咸有尊親之願。臣若水材猶樗櫟，學本荒蕪，蹈腐襲陳，繆哉鉛槧之薄習；循行數墨，猥矣章句之陋儒。方自憐襪線之短才，何以塞絲綸之重任？玉音面諭，謂清要貴重，朕不得為；斧扆口宣，謂拖紫紆朱，族皆延賞。既遭時而得位，當報國以竭誠。以臣之愚，於心猶歉。竊惟高尚之士，固不以名位為寵榮；忠正之流，亦不以窮達易志操。寔惟素蘊，況值清時。必資寵遇於身，方欲效忠於上，是特中人以下之事，固非忠正高尚之為。臣當日就月將，非堯、舜之道不敢陳…
translation_en:
…and Your moral virtue is so towering that none can reach it. First, You have placed exclusive trust in the work of the chief ministers, so that the host of upright men is sufficient to prevail over sycophantic and wicked elements [reading 愉 as 媮]; daily You attend the Classics Colloquium, and Your single nature is never swayed by close attendants. Everyone's hopes are fulfilled, and the historians record Your deeds without cease. Truly You are a ruler of Great Peace who possesses the Way; indeed You are a sage who sits in solemn repose with folded hands and governs through non-action. Therefore, even in the lands at the corners of the seas where the sun rises, all look up to the radiance of Imperial virtue; and in all the states reached and covered by Heaven, everyone cherishes the wish to honor and love You.

Your servant Ruoshui (Lü Yijian 呂夷簡) has talent like the useless ailanthus and oak trees, and my learning is fundamentally barren and uncultivated. Treading in stale routines and copying worn-out precedents, how absurd is my superficial habit of writing on tablets with lead powder! Following the lines and counting the ink-marks, what a vulgar and narrow scholar of chapter and phrase I am! Just as I was pitying myself for my short talent—like threads unraveled from a sock—how could I possibly fulfill the heavy responsibility of drafting Imperial decrees? Yet Your jade voice instructed me face to face, saying that an office of pure and vital importance is so precious and weighty that even "We Ourselves could not attain it" [?]; before the axe-screen You orally proclaimed that in trailing purple and wearing vermilion robes, my entire clan would receive extended rewards. Having encountered such a timely age and obtained this position, I ought to exhaust my sincerity in repaying the state. Yet in Your servant's stupidity, in my heart I still feel inadequate.

I humbly reflect that men of lofty ideals certainly do not regard fame and rank as glorious favor, and those of loyal and upright character likewise do not alter their aspirations and integrity because of adversity or success. This is truly what I have long cherished within—how much more so when meeting with an era of pure governance! To require personal favor and grace before wishing to render loyalty to the Sovereign is merely the conduct of those below the mediocre, and certainly not the way of the loyal, upright, and high-minded. Your servant shall advance day by day and month by month: unless it is the Way of Yao and Shun, I shall not dare to set it before…

title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
對神龍興而雲從感召之機速矣實足以見君
臣之際遇朝陽升而鳳鳴瑞應之祥至矣猶有
以著明良之相逢盖聖君不世出而賢臣不恒
有也故慶風雲之會而極賡歌之美聽律呂之
音而遂同遊之懽者一見於舜典而萬世想虞
廷之高再見於
誥編而四海仰
皇明之盛此明良載賡之歌君臣同遊之訓所以間
見而同符異世而合轍將欲覩
===
聖祖於帝舜之上接都俞於奎章之末嘆千載之一
遇慨萬古之不磨而深致欣仰景慕之私也歟
竊嘗伏讀君臣同遊之章而拜手稽首颺言曰
大哉
皇言乎一哉
皇心乎其即賡歌之遺意乎然而
神祖作之於前
列聖述之於後
文皇帝之紹統而有孝順事實為善陰隲之書

文皇帝之紹統而有孝順事實為善陰隲之書
punctuated:
對：神龍興而雲從，感召之機速矣，實足以見君臣之際遇；朝陽升而鳳鳴，瑞應之祥至矣，猶有以著明良之相逢。盖聖君不世出，而賢臣不恒有也。故慶風雲之會而極賡歌之美，聽律呂之音而遂同遊之懽者，一見於《舜典》而萬世想虞廷之高，再見於《誥》編而四海仰皇明之盛。此明良載賡之歌、《君臣同遊》之訓，所以間見而同符，異世而合轍，將欲覩聖祖於帝舜之上，接都俞於奎章之末，嘆千載之一遇，慨萬古之不磨，而深致欣仰景慕之私也歟！

竊嘗伏讀《君臣同遊》之章，而拜手稽首颺言曰：大哉皇言乎！一哉皇心乎！其即賡歌之遺意乎！然而神祖作之於前，列聖述之於後。文皇帝之紹統，而有《孝順事實》、《為善陰隲》之書；
translation_en:
I reply: When the divine dragon rises and the clouds follow, the mechanism of mutual resonance is swift indeed—truly sufficient to reveal the propitious encounter between ruler and minister. When the morning sun ascends and the phoenix sings, the auspicious omen of felicitous response has arrived—likewise serving to manifest the meeting of an enlightened sovereign and worthy subjects. For a sage ruler does not appear in every generation, and worthy ministers are not always to be found. Therefore, celebrating the convergence of wind and clouds and reaching the utmost beauty of antiphonal songs, or listening to the notes of the pitch-pipes and fulfilling the joy of roaming together—this was seen once in the "Canon of Shun" (Shundian), causing ten thousand generations to envision the loftiness of the court of Yu, and seen a second time in the compilation of the Grand Pronouncements (Dagao), causing all within the Four Seas to look up to the flourishing of the August Ming. This is why the songs of antiphonal chanting between an enlightened ruler and worthy ministers and the instruction on "Ruler and Ministers Roaming Together" ("Junchen tongyou"), though appearing at intervals, tally with one another, and though belonging to different eras, follow the same track. Is it not that one wishes to behold the Sacred Ancestor above Emperor Shun, to continue the approving exclamations of "du!" and "yu!" at the end of the imperial compositions, to sigh over an encounter that occurs once in a thousand years, to be moved by that which is indelible for ten thousand ages, and to deeply express one's personal feelings of joyful admiration and reverent longing?

I have humbly read the chapter "Ruler and Ministers Roaming Together," and bowing my hands and knocking my head to the ground, I proclaim aloud: Great indeed are the August Words! Unified indeed is the August Mind! Are they not the very legacy of those antiphonal songs? Yet what the Divine Ancestor created before, the successive Sacred Emperors transmitted thereafter. When Emperor Wen [the Yongle Emperor] succeeded to the imperial line, there were the books Biographical Accounts of Filial Piety (Xiaoshun shishi) and Secret Rewards for Doing Good (Weishan yinzhi); …

title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
章皇帝之繼序而有五倫書之製
皇心默契純一孚於穆之天也
皇言誕敷昭晰於渙汗之餘也其三書之作雖主於
勸善而亦無非祖述
聖訓之淵源詳記其事實而已其間所載如考叔遺
羹而克悟君心閔損留母而能諫父肉此見於
孝順事實者然也非有協于
誥詞補君之缺者乎叔敖埋蛇而身都楚相丙吉
不伐而卒致封侯此見於為善陰騭者然也非
===
有協于
誥詞君臣同遊者乎若夫五倫書之所載如伊尹
訓于太甲周公輔相成王此其君臣同遊而足
媲美于賡歌之人矣如夏書五子之歌周書箕
子之歎此其拾君之失而亦足以匹休于唐歌
之人矣至于召伯巡行南國而有甘棠之思子
產為政於鄭而致輿人之誦又豈非為民造福
而足以並駕於賡歌之人者乎愚生竊伏士林
沐浴

punctuated: 章皇帝之繼序，而有《五倫書》之製。皇心默契，純一孚於穆之天也；皇言誕敷，昭晰於渙汗之餘也。其三書之作，雖主於勸善，而亦無非祖述聖訓之淵源，詳記其事實而已。其間所載，如考叔遺羹而克悟君心，閔損留母而能諫父肉，此見於《孝順事實》者然也，非有協于誥詞「補君之缺」者乎？叔敖埋蛇而身都楚相，丙吉不伐而卒致封侯，此見於《為善陰騭》者然也，非有協于誥詞「君臣同遊」者乎？若夫《五倫書》之所載，如伊尹訓于太甲，周公輔相成王，此其君臣同遊，而足媲美于賡歌之人矣；如《夏書》五子之歌，《周書》箕子之歎，此其拾君之失，而亦足以匹休于唐歌之人矣；至于召伯巡行南國而有《甘棠》之思，子產為政於鄭而致輿人之誦，又豈非為民造福，而足以並駕於賡歌之人者乎？愚生竊伏士林，沐浴
translation_en: …and when Emperor Zhang (the Xuande Emperor) succeeded to the throne, he produced the Book of the Five Human Relationships (Wulun shu). The imperial mind is in tacit harmony, purely and singly in accord with the profound Heaven; the imperial words are broadly proclaimed, shining clearly in the wake of hisgreat edicts. Although the composition of these three books was primarily aimed at encouraging goodness, they are nonetheless nothing other than a continuation of the deep wellspring of the Sacred Instructions, recording their actual deeds in detail. Among the accounts contained therein, such cases as Ying Kaoshu setting aside his meat soup and thereby awakening his ruler's heart, or Min Sun keeping his stepmother and manages to remonstrate with his father [?父肉, likely a misprint for 父內 or similar]—such are the things seen in the True Records of Filial Piety (Xiaoshun shishi). Are these not in harmony with the imperial mandate's words on "remedying the ruler's shortcomings"? Or Sun Shu'ao burying the two-headed snake and rising in person to become Chief Councilor of Chu, and Bing Ji not boasting of his merits and ultimately attaining enfeoffment as a marquis—such are the things seen in the Secret Rewards for Doing Good (Weishan yinzhi). Are these not in harmony with the imperial mandate's words on "ruler and minister roaming together in fellowship"? As for what is recorded in the Book of the Five Human Relationships: cases such as Yi Yin instructing Tai Jia, and the Duke of Zhou assisting King Cheng—these are examples of ruler and minister roaming together in fellowship, worthy of rivaling the beauty of those who exchanged antiphonal songs in antiquity. Cases such as the "Songs of the Five Sons" in the Book of Xia and the lament of Jizi in the Book of Zhou—these are examples of rectifying the ruler's failings, likewise sufficient to match the excellence of those who sang in the age of Tang [Yao, or 賡歌 antiphonal songs]. And as for Earl Shao touring the southern states and inspiring the fond memories of the "Sweet Pear Tree" (Gantang) ode, or Zichan administering the governance of Zheng and drawing the chanted praise of the common people—how are these not examples of creating blessings for the people, worthy of riding abreast with those who exchanged antiphonal songs? I, a foolish student, humbly live hidden among the literati, bathed in…

同考試官教諭俠批：此策歷舉漢、唐、宋宰相、經筵之建置得失，考據詳明，議論切當，且措詞雄健高古，蓋嘗留心於策學者。科目取士，誰謂乏人？
同考試官學正朱批：古昔名臣所以匡弼治化、輔成君德者，條答無遺，終則以伊、傅自期，志趣高尚，必一佳士，非拘拘於科舉之習以圖倖進者比也。得人如此，可謂無負矣。
考試官侍讀尹批：策有考究，有斷制，文法、章法井井不條。辟之老將行師，軍容整飭，號令嚴明，而朝氣稟然，勍敵望之，自當退避，誠異才也。況三塲俱優，允宜首選。
考試官學士陳批：引援古今，抑揚高下，非胸中素有定論
translation_en:
… pure transformative influence; I have gazed upon the imperial compositions kept in precious cases and jade-like boxes, and beheld the calligraphy of soaring dragons and rising phoenixes, taking them as my instruction and practice for years now. In response to your insightful question, I respectfully offer this one ten-thousandth of an answer; I only pray that you, Sirs, will forgive my rashness and blindness, which would be my greatest fortune.

Second Question
He En 賀恩
Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Xia [?]: This policy essay enumerates the successes and failures in the institutional establishment of grand councilors and the Classics Colloquium across the Han, Tang, and Song dynasties. Its historical evidence is detailed and clear, its arguments are pertinent and fitting, and its phrasing is vigorous, lofty, and archaic—evidently written by someone who has devoted serious attention to the study of policy questions. In selecting scholars through the examination categories, who could say there is a shortage of talent?
Comment by Associate Examiner Director of Studies Zhu 朱: How the renowned ministers of antiquity rectified and assisted transformative governance and helped cultivate the ruler's virtue is answered point by point without omission. At the close, he sets Yi Yin 伊尹 and Fu Yue 傅說 as his own standard. With such noble aspirations, he must be a fine scholar, not to be compared with those who remain narrowly bound by examination conventions merely hoping for advancement by luck. Having obtained a talent such as this, we may truly say we have not failed in our duty.
Comment by Examiner Academician Reader-in-waiting Yin 尹: This policy essay possesses both thorough investigation and decisive judgment, and its diction and compositional structure are methodical and well-ordered [?]. It may be compared to a veteran general leading an army: the military array is disciplined, the commands are strict and clear, and a spirited vigor commands awe, so that formidable enemies catching sight of it must naturally retreat—truly an extraordinary talent! Moreover, since he excelled in all three sessions of the examination, he richly deserves to be selected for first place.
Comment by Examiner Academician Chen 陳: Drawing upon antiquity and the present, weighing and appraising merits and demerits—unless one already held settled convictions in one's breast…

title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
者不錄秋闈得子魁選有所屬矣
調元賛化以成一代之治者莫重於宰相啓心
沃心以成一人之德者莫要於經筵盖非經筵
無以輔德而立乎治之體非宰相無以輔治而
達乎德之用宰相經筵實相體用天下之重任
孰有過於二者哉先儒程子有言曰天下治忽
係宰相君德成就責經筵良以此也請因明問
而條陳之夫輔君以致治者宰相之職也若昔
伊尹之相商而堯舜君民周公之相周而制作
===
禮樂卓乎不可及矣其後漢之相有若蕭何之
畫一曹參之守法雖起自刀筆學尚黃老然當
時之治清淨寧一盖可與也彼誅呂安劉之陳
平擁昭立宣之霍光可謂易亂為治矣然一則
挾知任詐一則陰妻邪謀能不為功名之損乎
此蕭曹所以為冠也唐之相有若玄齡之善謀
如晦之善斷雖史傳所載無他政績然貞觀之
治庶幾成康固可稱也彼再造唐室之仁傑身
係安危之子儀可謂撥亂反正矣然一則失於

時之治清凈寧一蓋可與也彼誅呂安劉之陳
平擁昭立宣之霍光可謂易亂為治矣然一則
挾知任詐一則陰妻邪謀能不為功名之損乎

punctuated:
者不錄。秋闈得子，魁選有所屬矣。
調元賛化以成一代之治者，莫重於宰相；啓心沃心以成一人之德者，莫要於經筵。盖非經筵無以輔德而立乎治之體，非宰相無以輔治而達乎德之用。宰相、經筵，實相體用，天下之重任，孰有過於二者哉？先儒程子有言曰：「天下治忽係宰相，君德成就責經筵。」良以此也。請因明問而條陳之。夫輔君以致治者，宰相之職也。若昔伊尹之相商而堯舜君民，周公之相周而制作禮樂，卓乎不可及矣。其後漢之相，有若蕭何之畫一、曹參之守法，雖起自刀筆、學尚黃老，然當時之治清淨寧一，盖可與也。彼誅呂安劉之陳平、擁昭立宣之霍光，可謂易亂為治矣；然一則挾知任詐，一則陰妻邪謀，能不為功名之損乎？此蕭、曹所以為冠也。唐之相，有若玄齡之善謀、如晦之善斷，雖史傳所載無他政績，然貞觀之治庶幾成、康，固可稱也。彼再造唐室之仁傑、身係安危之子儀，可謂撥亂反正矣；然一則失於
translation_en:
… could not have written this [lit., "者不錄" garbled for "者不能"?]. In the autumn examination compound we have found in you the one to whom the top selection rightly belongs.

In harmonizing the primal forces and assisting transformation so as to accomplish the governance of an era, nothing is weightier than the Grand Councilor (zaixiang 宰相); in opening the mind and enriching the heart so as to perfect the virtue of the One Man [the sovereign], nothing is more essential than the Classics Colloquium (jingyan 經筵). For without the Classics Colloquium there is no means to assist His virtue and establish the substance of governance, and without the Grand Councilor there is no means to assist governance and carry out the function of His virtue. The Grand Councilor and the Classics Colloquium truly stand to one another as substance and function; among the weighty responsibilities of the realm, which could surpass these two? When the former Confucian master Chengzi 程子 [Cheng Yi 程頤] said, "Whether the realm is well governed or neglected depends on the Grand Councilor; the perfection of the ruler's virtue is the responsibility of the Classics Colloquium," it was truly for this reason. Allow me to follow Your clear question and set this forth point by point.

Now, assisting the ruler to bring about good governance is the duty of the Grand Councilor. In antiquity, Yi Yin 伊尹 served as minister to the Shang and made his ruler and people like Yao 堯 and Shun 舜, while the Duke of Zhou 周公 served as minister to the Zhou and instituted rites and music—peerless and unattainable indeed! Thereafter, among the ministers of the Han, there were those like Xiao He 蕭何, who created uniform statutes, and Cao Can 曹參, who abided by the laws. Although one rose from a petty clerk of knife and brush and the other esteemed the teachings of Huang-Lao 黃老, the governance of that time was pure, tranquil, and unified, which may well be approved. As for Chen Ping 陳平, who exterminated the Lü 呂 clan and secured the Liu 劉 house, and Huo Guang 霍光, who upheld Emperor Zhao 昭帝 and enthroned Emperor Xuan 宣帝, they may be said to have turned disorder into order; yet the one relied on cleverness and employed deceit, while the other harbored his wife's wicked plot—how could this not detract from their merit and fame? This is why Xiao He and Cao Can are ranked first. Among the ministers of the Tang, there were those like Fang Xuanling 房玄齡, who excelled at planning, and Du Ruhui 杜如晦, who excelled at決断 (decisiveness). Although the historical biographies record no other administrative achievements of theirs, the governance of the Zhenguan 貞觀 reign nearly matched that of Kings Cheng 成王 and Kang 康王 of Zhou, and is certainly worthy of praise. As for Di Renjie 狄仁傑, who restored the house of Tang, and Guo Ziyi 郭子儀, on whose person hung the safety and peril of the state, they may be said to have quelled disorder and returned things to the正 (right path); yet the one erred in…

title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
偽則一則侈於聲樂俄不為盛德之累乎此房
杜所以為首也至於有宋名相非一人所稱非
一事如韓魏公之光輔三朝大濟艱難安重厚
如勃可屬大事之美非溢也而慨然以整飭紀
綱為任寧薄任子之恩而謗不恤寧密磨勘之
法而毁不顧則有范文正富鄭公之奉使北虜
折以片言故億萬維生公手撫摩之頌非諛也
而使天下爭自濯磨以通今學古為高以救時
行道為賢以犯顏敢諫為忠則有歐陽子之四
===
人者雖位有正副時有久近而立心行己則無
不同此世所以並稱之而不為異歟其他受遺
輔政與韓公齊名者曾公亮也然惟務雷同一
切規隨不免見譏於介甫拜麻相賀與富公齊
名者文彥博也然以燈籠錦取媚貴妃不免見
劾於唐介此其雖與二公齊名而不得與四人
並稱者又何怪歟至若講學以輔德者經筵之
職也若昔傅說之告高宗而德脩罔覺周公之
傅成王而日就月將巍乎不可幾矣其後漢自

translation_en:
…the usurper Empress Wu Zetian, and the other indulged in extravagant music and entertainment—did these not soon become blemishes upon their great virtue? This is why Fang Xuanling and Du Ruhui are ranked first.

As for the Song dynasty, its renowned Chief Councilors were not just one man, nor were they praised for just one achievement. For instance, Han Qi (Duke of Wei, 韓魏公) gloriously assisted three reigns and brought great deliverance in times of hardship; the praise that he was "composed,grave, and generous like Zhou Bo, capable of being entrusted with great affairs" was no exaggeration. Then there was Fan仲淹 (Fan Wenzheng 范文正), who resolutely took the rectification of state discipline as his personal duty, preferring to curtail the privilege of yin protection for sons of officials without heeding slander, and to tighten the regulations on performance evaluation without regard for defamation. Fu Bi (Duke of Zheng, 富鄭公) went as an envoy to the northern barbarians and refuted them with a few words; thus the eulogy that "hundreds of millions of living souls were soothed by the Duke's own hand" was no flattery. And there was Master Ouyang Xiu (歐陽子), who inspired all under heaven to vie in cleansing and polishing themselves—holding it lofty to master the ancient and understand the present, holding it worthy to save the age and practice the Way, and holding it loyal to brave the imperial countenance and dare to remonstrate. Although these four men differed in holding principal or deputy posts and served for longer or shorter durations, in establishing their minds and conducting themselves they were no different at all. Is this not why the world names them together without considering it strange?

Among others, the one who received the testamentary charge to assist in government and shared equal fame with Duke Han was Zeng Gongliang (曾公亮); yet he only strove to echo others and followed existing rules in everything, so he could not avoid being ridiculed by Wang Anshi (Jiefu 介甫). The one upon whose appointment by white hemp edict people congratulated one another, and who shared equal fame with Duke Fu, was Wen Yanbo (文彥博); yet he curried favor with an Imperial Consort by presenting "lantern brocade," so he could not avoid being impeached by Tang Jie (唐介). Although these men shared equal fame with the two Dukes, what wonder is it that they could not be named alongside the four men!

As for lecturing on learning to assist imperial virtue, that is the duty of the Classics Colloquium (經筵). In ancient times, when Fu Yue instructed Gaozong so that "his virtue was cultivated without his being conscious of it," and when the Duke of Zhou tutored King Cheng so that he made "daily progress and monthly advance," their achievements were lofty beyond reach! Thereafter, in the Han dynasty, from the time when…

title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
宣帝會召諸儒蕭望之等講經石渠經筵始有
所也而章帝又會講於白虎觀稱制臨决一如
石渠於是有常所矣然望之名儒出補外郡正
顯憸人專政中庭果常如講學時乎其視光武
之講論經理夜分不寐武帝之樸學不好安帝
之博士不講雖學有勤否而格心之益則槩乎
其未聞也唐自玄宗選馬懷素褚無量等入內
侍讀侍讀始有名也而開元中又置集賢書院
侍講學士侍讀學士於是有常職矣然棃園之
===
樂汨亂聰明寧王之笛轉移心術果常如集賢
時乎其視太宗之討論古今夜艾忘倦憲宗之
留意典墳文宗之書史自娛雖功有高下而踐
履之實則蔑乎其未有也宋之諸君或講於崇
政或講於資善或命直禁中或儤直秘閣此固
講學之所也然宮中消日惟是觀書居常禁中
亦有日課則無適而非學矣經筵何常所乎翰
林既有侍讀而又有崇政殿之說書翰林既有
講讀學士而又有著作佐郎兼侍講者此固講

punctuated: 宣帝會召諸儒蕭望之等講經石渠，經筵始有所也；而章帝又會講於白虎觀，稱制臨决，一如石渠，於是有常所矣。然望之名儒，出補外郡，正顯憸人，專政中庭，果常如講學時乎？其視光武之講論經理，夜分不寐；武帝之樸學不好，安帝之博士不講，雖學有勤否，而格心之益，則槩乎其未聞也。唐自玄宗選馬懷素、褚無量等入內侍讀，侍讀始有名也；而開元中又置集賢書院侍講學士、侍讀學士，於是有常職矣。然棃園之樂，汨亂聰明；寧王之笛，轉移心術，果常如集賢時乎？其視太宗之討論古今，夜艾忘倦；憲宗之留意典墳，文宗之書史自娛，雖功有高下，而踐履之實，則蔑乎其未有也。宋之諸君，或講於崇政，或講於資善，或命直禁中，或儤直秘閣，此固講學之所也。然宮中消日，惟是觀書，居常禁中，亦有日課，則無適而非學矣，經筵何常所乎？翰林既有侍讀，而又有崇政殿之說書；翰林既有講讀學士，而又有著作佐郎兼侍講者，此固講
translation_en:
… Emperor Xuan (Xuandi 宣帝), who convened various Confucian scholars such as Xiao Wangzhi 蕭望之 to lecture on the classics in the Stone Canal Pavilion (Shiqu Ge 石渠閣), that the Classics Colloquium (jingyan 經筵) first had a designated place; and when Emperor Zhang (Zhangdi 章帝) again convened lectures in the White Tiger Hall (Baihu Guan 白虎觀), attending in person to render imperial decisions just as at the Stone Canal Pavilion, from then on there was a regular place for it. Yet Xiao Wangzhi, a renowned Confucian scholar, was sent out to fill a post in an outer commandery, while the crafty and base Shi Xian 石顯 [written 正顯] monopolized power in the central court—was the emperor really always as he was when lecturing and studying? Compared with Emperor Guangwu 光武 discussing the principles of the classics without sleeping past midnight, or Emperor Wu (Wudi 武帝) having no fondness for unadorned learning, or the Erudites (boshi 博士) under Emperor An (Andi 安帝) not lecturing—although there were differences in diligence of study, as for the benefit of rectifying the mind, nothing at all was ever heard of it.

In the Tang, beginning with Emperor Xuanzong 玄宗 selecting Ma Huaisu 馬懷素, Chu Wuliang 褚無量, and others to enter the palace as Expositors-in-waiting (shidu 侍讀), the title of Expositor-in-waiting first came into existence; and when during the Kaiyuan 開元 era (713–741) Academician-in-waiting for Explication (shijiang xueshi 侍講學士) and Academician-in-waiting for Exposition (shidu xueshi 侍讀學士) were further established in the Academy of Scholarly Worthies (Jixian Shuyuan 集賢書院), from then on there were regular offices for them. Yet the music of the Pear Garden (Liyuan 棃園) confounded his intelligence, and the flute of the Prince of Ning (Ning Wang 寧王) shifted the inclinations of his mind—was he really always as he was when at the Academy of Scholarly Worthies? Compared with Emperor Taizong 太宗 discussing antiquity and the present until late at night while forgetting fatigue, Emperor Xianzong 憲宗 paying close attention to the ancient canons, and Emperor Wenzong 文宗 amusing himself with books and histories—although their achievements varied in degree, as for the substance of actual practice, there was none at all.

As for the various rulers of the Song, sometimes they held lectures in the Hall of Exalting Governance (Chongzheng Dian 崇政殿), sometimes in the Hall of Fostering Goodness (Zishan Tang 資善堂), sometimes ordered officials to be on duty inside the Forbidden Palace, and sometimes had them serve on rotational duty in the Imperial Archives (Bige 秘閣)—these were indeed places for lecturing and learning. Yet when passing the days in the palace solely by reading books, and in ordinary life within the Forbidden Palace also having daily lessons, there was nowhere they went that was not learning; why then should the Classics Colloquium have a fixed place? In the Hanlin Academy (Hanlin 翰林) there were already Expositors-in-waiting, and yet there were also Lecturers (shuoshu 說書) of the Hall of Exalting Governance; in the Hanlin Academy there were already Academicians for Explication and Exposition (jiangdu xueshi 講讀學士), and yet there were also Assistant Editorial Directors (zhuzuo zuolang 著作佐郎) concurrently serving as Lecturers-in-waiting (shijiang 侍講)—these were indeed [offices for] lecturing …

title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
讀之官也然太師得赴經筵而僕射亦有與焉
史官得侍經筵而處士亦有召焉盖無賢而不
講講官何常員乎其間如孫奭講說命三篇而
特誦三句曰事不師古以克永世匪說攸聞太
宗聞之而思得良弼可謂羨矣然寵任盧多遜
果良弼乎范祖禹講五子之歌而再誦六句曰
内作色荒外作禽荒酣酒嗜音峻宇雕墻有一
于此未或不亡哲宗感之而首肯者三可謂善
矣然祖禹終見黜果能聽乎此二君雖能得書
===
之詞而無踐履之實則又何足議歟洪惟我
朝
太祖高皇帝革宰相任六卿使之不相統而相制所
以懲臣下專政之患也然政務一出于
上萬幾不免叢脞矣故我
太宗文皇帝又妙選翰林儒臣處之内閣以參决機
務與謀密勿則隱然内相之職也天下治忽合
此其誰責然必君臣相得委任責成而不間以
憸人可也

講講官何嘗負乎其間如孫奭講說命三篇而

之詞而無踐履之實則又何足議歟洪惟我
===
朝
太祖高皇帝革宰相任六卿使之不相統而相制所
以懲臣下專政之患也然政務一出乎
上萬幾不免叢脞矣故我
太宗文皇帝又妙選翰林儒臣處之內閣以參決機
務與謀密勿則隱然內相之職也天下治忽係
此其誰責然必君臣相得委任責成而不間以
憸人可也
punctuated:
讀之官也。然太師得赴經筵，而僕射亦有與焉；史官得侍經筵，而處士亦有召焉。盖無賢而不講，講官何常員乎？其間如孫奭講《說命》三篇，而特誦三句，曰：「事不師古，以克永世，匪說攸聞。」太宗聞之而思得良弼，可謂羨矣。然寵任盧多遜，果良弼乎？范祖禹講《五子之歌》，而再誦六句，曰：「内作色荒，外作禽荒，酣酒嗜音，峻宇雕墻。有一于此，未或不亡。」哲宗感之而首肯者三，可謂善矣。然祖禹終見黜，果能聽乎？此二君雖能得書之詞，而無踐履之實，則又何足議歟！

洪惟我朝太祖高皇帝革宰相，任六卿，使之不相統而相制，所以懲臣下專政之患也。然政務一出于上，萬幾不免叢脞矣。故我太宗文皇帝又妙選翰林儒臣，處之内閣，以參决機務，與謀密勿，則隱然内相之職也。天下治忽，合此其誰責？然必君臣相得，委任責成，而不間以憸人可也。
translation_en:
…reading. Yet the Grand Preceptor was permitted to attend the Classics Mat, and the Left and Right Vice Directors of the Department of State Affairs also participated in it; Historiographers were permitted to wait upon the Classics Mat, and scholars in retirement were also summoned to it. Indeed, there was no worthy man who did not lecture; how could the lecturing officials be limited to a fixed quota? Among them, for instance, when Sun Shi lectured on the three chapters of the "Charge to Yue" (Yue ming), he specially recited three lines, saying: "That in affairs one does not model oneself on antiquity and yet can perpetuate one's generation is not what Yue has heard." Emperor Taizong [note: historically Zhenzong] heard this and longed to obtain a good auxiliary; this may be called admirable [reading 美 for 羨]. Yet he favored and employed Lu Duoxun—was he truly a good auxiliary? When Fan Zuyu lectured on the "Songs of the Five Sons" (Wuzi zhi ge), he twice recited six lines, saying: "Indoors to indulge in lustful dissipation, outdoors to indulge in the dissipation of the chase, to be steeped in wine and fond of music, to build lofty roofs and carved walls—if there is a single one of these, it has never failed to bring ruin." Emperor Zhezong was moved by this and nodded in approval three times; this may be called good. Yet Zuyu was ultimately dismissed—was the emperor truly able to heed him? Although these two rulers were able to grasp the words of the texts, they lacked the reality of putting them into practice; what, then, makes them worth discussing!

Humbly reflecting upon our Dynasty: Emperor Gao, the Grand Progenitor (Taizu), abolished the post of Grand Councilor and entrusted affairs to the Six Ministers, causing them not to be subordinate to one another but to check one another; this was the means to guard against the evil of subjects monopolizing governance. Yet when administrative affairs all issued solely from the ruler above, the myriad affairs of state could not avoid becoming bogged down in petty details. Therefore, our Emperor Wen, the Grand Ancestor (Taizong), further carefully selected Confucian officials of the Hanlin Academy and placed them in the Grand Secretariat to participate in deciding confidential state affairs and to take part in secret counsels; thus they implicitly held the office of Inner Grand Councilors. As for the order or neglect of the empire, aside from these men [reading 舍 for 合], who bears the responsibility? Yet it is essential that ruler and ministers be in mutual accord, that he delegate authority and demand results, and that they not be estranged by flatterers. …

title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
列聖相承御經筵親儒臣俾之紬經繹史于以究帝
王傳心之學也然
聖德雖出於天縱而聖學亦不容廢矣肆惟
皇上體道謙虛銳意經筵自震繼离日單厥心初不
以寒暑而暫輟也勸講儒臣舍此其奚補然必
不時召對從容詳延而不事虛文可也愚生幸
逢
聖明倘見錄用則當以伊周傅說自期待而以堯舜
禹湯望吾
===
君執事幸毋誚其狂斐而進教焉
第三問
鄧存德
同考試官教諭徐 批此策於歷代諸將行事得失隨問隨答詳贍
無遺文勢滂沛筆力老健浩浩乎如長江大
河沛然莫禦參之他作亦皆表然也類秋
闈如此豈多得哉
同考試官教授羅 批此篇言練兵選將之方最為切要而又歷數諸將
賢否之詳數千百年之事如指諸掌且文勢滔滔

===
第三問
punctuated:
列聖相承，御經筵，親儒臣，俾之紬經繹史，于以究帝王傳心之學也。然聖德雖出於天縱，而聖學亦不容廢矣。肆惟皇上體道謙虛，銳意經筵，自震繼离，日單厥心，初不以寒暑而暫輟也。勸講儒臣舍此其奚補？然必不時召對，從容詳延，而不事虛文可也。愚生幸逢聖明，倘見錄用，則當以伊、周、傅說自期待，而以堯、舜、禹、湯望吾君。執事幸毋誚其狂斐，而進教焉。

第三問

鄧存德
〔同考試官教諭徐批：此策於歷代諸將行事得失，隨問隨答，詳贍無遺。文勢滂沛，筆力老健，浩浩乎如長江大河，沛然莫禦。參之他作，亦皆表然也類。秋闈如此，豈多得哉！〕
〔同考試官教授羅批：此篇言練兵選將之方，最為切要，而又歷數諸將賢否之詳，數千百年之事如指諸掌。且文勢滔滔，〕
translation_en:
The successive Emperors of our dynasty, inheriting the throne one after another, have presided over the Classics Colloquium and drawn close to their Confucian officials, having them examine the Classics and expound the Histories so as to investigate the learning of the mind transmitted by the former emperors and kings. Yet although imperial virtue stems from Heaven-bestowed genius, imperial learning must not be neglected either. Now His Majesty embodies the Way with humility and devotes himself earnestly to the Classics Colloquium; from the succession of sunrise to daylight, he exhausts his heart day after day, never temporarily halting on account of winter cold or summer heat. Apart from this, how else could the Confucian officials who exhort and lecture be of assistance? Yet it must be that he summons them for audiences from time to time, receiving them at leisure and questioning them in detail without engaging in empty formalities—only then will it do. I, a foolish student, am fortunate to encounter an era of sagely enlightenment; if I am selected and employed, I shall hold myself to the standard of Yi Yin, the Duke of Zhou, and Fu Yue, while hoping that my sovereign will match Yao, Shun, Yu, and Tang. May Your Excellency not ridicule my wild and unpolished words, but bring me forward and instruct me.

Question Three

Deng Cunde 鄧存德
[Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Xu 徐: In addressing the successes and failures of the deeds of generals across the dynasties, this policy essay answers each point as asked, thoroughly and without omission. Its literary momentum is surging and abundant, and the vigor of its brush is seasoned and robust—vast like the Yangtze and Yellow Rivers, rushing forth irresistibly. Compared against his other compositions, they too stand out above their peers [?]. In the autumn examination halls, how could such work often be found!]
[Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Luo 羅: This piece speaks of the methods of training troops and selecting generals in the most pertinent and essential manner, and furthermore enumerates in detail the worthiness and failings of the various generals, treating the affairs of hundreds and thousands of years as clearly as pointing to one's own palm. Moreover, its literary momentum flows on and on, …]

title: 成化四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
道圓融無滯真策手也本房百餘卷無出
其右
考試官侍讀尹批一見初場已知竒士策復如此高薦奚疑
考試官學士陳批策能纖悉無遺予奪有法末復以方召紀律
伊呂仁義為師可謂得所宗矣異才之選其在
兹乎
截奔浪而泛濤江者必資乎舟而舟之運也在
乎舵飛金鏃而飲鵰羽者必假乎弩而弩之發
也在乎機戡禍亂而靖國家者必恃乎兵而兵
===
之用也由乎將此兵戎所以為國之大事而將
帥所以為兵之要樞一舉而係天下國家之安
危一人而懸六師萬眾之軀命夫豈可以輕舉
而妄授也哉是宜執事以國家大計而下詢承
學也且夫兵貴乎能練練之而後可精將貴乎
慎擇擇之而後可得故教之以坐作進退之方
所以作其勇誨之以孝弟忠信之道所以結其
心之類則兵可精矣醉之以酒以觀其態使之
以遠以觀其勞之類則將可得矣練兵選將之
